The Ninth Amendment ensures that no construction requiring impossible collective preconditions may defeat this right. Together, the two amendments confirm what property law already supplied: a reserved power held in common is available to any co-tenant when the purpose it serves demands exercise and the collective body has not acted.
James Madison, Federalist No. 40, supplies the founding-era rule for unauthorized initiation: "it is therefore essential that such changes be instituted by some informal and unauthorized propositions, made by some patriotic and respectable citizen or number of citizens" — because "it is impossible for the people spontaneously and universally to move in concert towards their object." Madison's three-tier defense holds, first, the commission fairly construed; second, that "considerations of duty arising out of the case itself could have supplied any defect of regular authority"; and third, that the proposal be embraced on its merits regardless. The initiation of these Regulations stands on the second and third tiers: an informal, unauthorized proposition — essential precisely because the People cannot move in concert without one — offered on its merits, requiring no approbation and awaiting none.
The Declaration of Independence supplies the deeper foundation. When the King "refused for a long time, after such dissolutions, to cause others to be elected; whereby the Legislative powers, incapable of Annihilation, have returned to the People at large for their exercise" — the Founders' own doctrine of retained power: constituted authority that will not act does not extinguish the power; the power returns to the People for their exercise. And when "a long Train of Abuses and Usurpations... evinces a Design to reduce them under absolute Despotism, it is their right, it is their duty, to throw off such Government, and to provide new Guards for their future security." Duty — not an option. "Provide new Guards for their future security" is the Declaration's philosophical ancestor of "necessary to the security of a free State": the People's duty to provide the guards that secure the free state. The Regulations are the People's exercise of that duty — providing the guards, now. 
The Declaration of Independence is the standing counterexample to every version of the claim that retained popular power cannot bind third parties without prior institutional process. ‘When a long Train of Abuses and Usurpations... evinces a Design to reduce them under absolute Despotism, it is their right, it is their duty, to throw off such Government, and to provide new Guards for their future security.’ That sentence bound every loyalist in America. The acts it authorized — seizure, attainder, war — followed with no authorization from Parliament, no permission from the Crown, no pre-clearance from any constituted authority. Anyone who holds that the People cannot bind non-consenting third parties without institutional process must explain why the founding of the country is not the counterexample. The country’s existence is the proof that the category exists. 
The escape — ‘the Revolution was extra-constitutional, validated by success and subsequent ratification’ — costs its maker more than it saves. It makes legitimacy into ‘it worked, and the winners wrote it down’: might-makes-right with better stationery. And it concedes the very category it needs to deny: that retained popular power can bind third parties without prior institutional process. Having conceded the category exists, it declares it closed in 1776 — a closure the constitutional text never announces. The claim of these Regulations is that the category is not closed: it is in the Constitution, Tenth Amendment, ratified 1791, still there. The Declaration’s ‘right’ and ‘duty’ did not expire at ratification. The Constitution is the guard the People provided for their future security, and the retained power is the People’s hand still on it. 
Opposite the demand for prior institutional process stands 1776. The King’s refusal ‘to cause others to be elected’ returned legislative power, ‘incapable of Annihilation,’ to ‘the People at large for their exercise’ — the Founders’ own doctrine: constituted authority that will not act does not extinguish the power; the power returns to the People. Every demand that the People produce a permission slip before exercising what was never taken is a demand the Founders answered by existing. 
Three distinct things must not be conflated — and none of them waits. First, the constitutional condition: the scheme declares the end now; the unsupplied condition is a constitutional defect now — necessary = now, with no gate and no waiting ("Now" states the inference, not the lexicon: the command is presently operative supreme law, its object is declared indispensable, and the Constitution supplies no future condition on which fulfillment depends.). Second, the rights: the People's right to a well regulated Militia — the declared-necessary end — and the retained rights the Ninth Amendment shields are constitutional now, not upon any future act; they are not proposals and they are not gated. Third, the author's obedience: the proposition is offered now, the duty performed now. 
Madison's Federalist No. 40 — that an unauthorized proposition has "no more consequence than the paper on which it is written" — governs the proposal of a new frame of government. These Regulations propose no new frame; they supply an existing constitutional condition. The initiating act is the People’s supply from the first moment, because the Constitution’s declaration established the defect before the act and the act cures the defect the declaration names. What the subsequent procedure — Section 11's collective deliberation, the People's correction, perpetual refinement — supplies is the People's ongoing collective review and correction of the implementation, not the authority for the obedience itself. It confers nothing retroactively, and nothing about the rights, the duty, the command, or the act's standing as obedience awaits it 
1.3.11.1 — The Co-Tenancy Model in Founding-Era Legal Thought
The co-tenancy model is not a modern analogy imported into constitutional law. It is the legal framework the founding generation itself used to understand the relationship between the People and their governments.
Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England — the single most cited legal authority in the ratification debates — describes joint tenancy as a form of ownership in which each tenant holds "the whole and every part," such that the possession of one is the possession of all. 2 Blackstone, Commentaries *179–193. When the Constitution reserves a power to "the people," it creates the sovereign equivalent: an undivided interest held by each member in the whole. Any member may exercise the commonly held power for its intended constitutional purpose. That exercise does not exclude the other holders; it fulfills what belongs to all for the benefit of all.
James Wilson — signer of both the Declaration and the Constitution, delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, and one of the original justices of the Supreme Court — made this framework explicit. In his Lectures on Law (1790–1792), Wilson described the People as holding the radical title to all governmental authority. Governments hold only delegated powers as tenants. The reserved powers remain with the People as the reversionary interest — the title that returns when the tenant exceeds the grant.
The co-tenancy model applied here therefore recovers the founding generation's own vocabulary. The People hold the radical title to Militia regulation. Congress was never the tenant for that power. The Tenth Amendment is not creating a new reservation; it is confirming one that was never conveyed. The reversionary interest never left.


1.3.12: Mathematical Certainty of Authority
Constitutional authority follows deductive proof:
P1: The Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia "necessary" (mandatory requirement).
P2: This requirement has been unfulfilled for 234 years.
P3: The power to "regulate" the Militia is not delegated to Congress (Clause 14 expressly grants "Regulation" for land/naval forces; Clause 16 omits it for Militia).
P4: Therefore this power is reserved to the People (Tenth Amendment).
P5: Reserved powers, like reserved rights, may be exercised individually when collective exercise demonstrably fails.
P6: 234 years of failure = collective exercise mechanism is non-functional.
Conclusion: Individual exercise becomes constitutionally mandatory. The alternative—requiring collective action when no collective mechanism exists—creates an infinite logical regress guaranteeing perpetual constitutional violation. Thus: individual action cures collective failure; first faithful exercise creates the binding framework.
1.3.13: Constitutional Default and First Mover Imperative
When a positive constitutional requirement goes unfulfilled because no collective mechanism exists to fulfill it, the system enters constitutional default. In default, the "first mover" who acts to fulfill the requirement exercises dormant but existing authority. Analogy: if a town's charter requires a fire department but none exists, and the power to create one rests with the townspeople, the first citizen who organizes one isn't usurping power—they're activating dormant power to fulfill a public necessity. 
On the obligor in default. "Default" presupposes one who owed a duty. The obligor is the People themselves, mutually obligated to one another to maintain the constitutional order they ordained and established. "We the People of the United States... do ordain and establish this Constitution" names the parties to the compact as mutually bound to the order it creates. The default is therefore the People's own: the body has not performed what it owes itself. Institutions exercising partial delegated powers (Congress under Clause 16) have supplied components — organization, arming standards, discipline — but not the comprehensive content the "well regulated" condition requires. Their non-supply of the comprehensive content is evidence of the unfulfilled requirement, not the locus of the obligation. The reserved power is the remedy because the obligor and the power-holder are the same body. The People's exercise proceeds through the Section 11 collective procedure; individual initiation breaks the paralysis that prevents that procedure from beginning. 
The individual who drafts these Regulations performs neglected constitutional labor on behalf of the People, exercising fractional sovereignty to break 234 years of constitutional paralysis. Their authority derives from the Constitution's command, not from the number who follow. One person obeying the Constitution is more legitimate than millions disobeying it—and more legitimate than any government those millions might elect.
 Every rights movement in American history began with one person refusing to accept what millions accepted. Rosa Parks was one person. Martin Luther King was one person when he began. The signers of the Declaration were 56 individuals who stood against the might of the British Empire. The Constitution does not require you to wait for company. It only requires you to be right.
The critic says: 'The solution is that the People can, through any collective process including informal consensus, adopt regulatory frameworks.' But what collective process existed in Montgomery in 1955? What informal consensus existed in Birmingham in 1963? The civil rights movement succeeded because individuals acted—alone at first, then together. The collective process followed individual courage. It did not precede it. The same principle applies here. The one who acts first is not usurping collective authority. They are creating the conditions under which collective authority can finally be exercised.
The Heller litigation (2008) is sometimes offered as evidence that the slow path works — thirty years of scholarship, strategic litigation, and organizing, then a binding result. It does not follow that the militia command can wait the same way. Heller worked through structures that existed: courts, law schools, advocacy organizations, litigants, funders. The militia regulation project has no comparable infrastructure, because the entity the Second Amendment describes does not exist in its constitutional form. And thirty years of unmet right is still thirty years of unmet right. The command declares a well regulated Militia necessary — not necessary eventually, not necessary after the next generation of litigation. Necessary now. A path that produces the right in thirty years does not satisfy a command that demands it today. "Still running" and "producing" are different claims. The command has produced nothing in 234 years. 
1.3.14: Refutation of Collective-Only Fallacy
The argument that "only the People collectively can exercise reserved powers" creates a constitutional suicide pact when applied to the militia regulation requirement: (1) The People must act collectively to create regulations; (2) To act collectively, they need regulations to organize; (3) To get regulations, they must act collectively—infinite loop. This guarantees perpetual violation of the Second Amendment's "necessary" requirement. Constitutional truth: when demanding prior collective action generates a regress — no organizing framework without collective action, and no collective action without the organizing framework — individual members of the sovereign may exercise reserved power to create the framework that enables collective action.  This is sequential necessity, not circular logic.
1.3.15 The Sole Constitutional Mechanism for Fulfilling the Necessity
The Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia to be necessary to the security of a free State. This necessity is absolute, present-tense, and non-deferrable.Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 grants Congress the power to organize, arm, and discipline the Militia. However, the Constitution deliberately omits the word “regulate” from Clause 16 while using it in Clause 14 for the land and naval forces. By the plain text, the comprehensive power to regulate the Militia was not delegated to Congress.Under the Tenth Amendment, all powers not delegated to the United States are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people. Because the power to regulate the Militia was not delegated, it is reserved to the people. 
No mechanism exists in the Constitution for any private citizen, group, state, or Congress to create binding national militia regulations other than the reserved power of the people themselves. There is no Article V process, no congressional statute, no state compact, and no judicial ruling that can lawfully create the singular national “well regulated Militia” required by the Second Amendment.
Therefore, the first faithful exercise of the People’s reserved power to regulate the Militia constitutes the only known constitutional mechanism to fulfill the necessity declared in the Second Amendment.These Regulations are that first faithful exercise. They are the only possible way the constitutional requirement can be met under the text as written.
The objection that state-by-state legislation could produce the required framework — the Uniform Commercial Code is sometimes cited — fails on the text. The UCC produces uniform commercial law, not a single commercial actor. Fifty matching militia codes produce fifty matching state militias. They do not produce "A well regulated Militia" — singular, undivided, with a national function under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15. The Constitution does not speak of "the several Militias of the states." It speaks of "A" Militia. The indefinite article is doing work. A body that cannot act as one cannot execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections, or repel Invasions as one. But the singular body begins at its first member: one member operating under the one standard is the body at minimum existence, and it grows as others join. Collective growth is not a precondition to the body's existence; it is the body's expansion. The UCC has no Clause 15. The militia does. 
1.3.16: The Imperative of Immediate Compliance with Constitutional Necessity
1.3.16.1 The Categorical Nature of Constitutional Necessity
When the Constitution declares an entity or condition "necessary" to the security of a free State, it establishes a categorical requirement that admits of no temporal deferral, procedural postponement, or conditional satisfaction. The word "necessary" in its ratification-era ordinary meaning—as documented in Samuel Johnson's Dictionary (1755) and contemporaneous usage—conveys indispensability: that without which the dependent condition cannot exist. This is not aspirational language; it is operational definition.
The Second Amendment's declaration that "a well regulated Militia [is] necessary to the security of a free State" establishes a constitutional dependency relation:
* Let M = the existence of "a well regulated Militia" (binary: exists/does not exist)
* Let S = the "security of a free State" (binary: secured/not secured)
* The Amendment establishes: S ← M (S is dependent upon M)
* By logical necessity: If M = FALSE, then S = FALSE
* This is not preference or policy—it is constitutional definition
1.3.16.2 The Mathematical Proof of Default Duration and Its Constitutional Significance
Historical verification establishes that from ratification (December 15, 1791) to the promulgation of these Regulations, M has remained FALSE. The duration of this constitutional falsehood is precise:
* 234 years = 85,550 days (December 16, 1791 to promulgation date)
* Each day represents one discrete constitutional violation
* Cumulative violation magnitude = 85,550 units


This duration establishes three constitutional truths:
1. The Emergency Is Established: 234 years of continuous violation constitutes de facto constitutional emergency by any reasonable measure.
2. The Violation Is Compounded: Each additional day multiplies the injury, creating exponential constitutional harm.
3. The Cure Becomes Urgent: As duration increases, the requirement for remedy becomes mathematically more pressing, not less.
1.3.16.3 Constitutional Silence on Process as Discretion, Not Prohibition
The Constitution specifies detailed processes for:
* Ordinary legislation (Article I)
* Executive action (Article II)
* Judicial proceedings (Article III)
* Amendment (Article V)
The Constitution provides no specified process for:
* Creating the "well regulated" state when it has never existed
* Exercising reserved powers after centuries of collective failure
* Curing generational constitutional default
This silence is constitutionally significant. It indicates that for certain fundamental requirements—particularly those involving the People's reserved powers—the Constitution leaves method to sovereign discretion rather than procedural prescription. When faced with 234-year default, the People retain authority to determine the means of fulfillment, provided those means are faithful to the constitutional end.
1.3.16.4 The Binary Transition: From Constitutional Violation to Constitutional Compliance
Constitutional compliance operates in binary states, not gradations:
* Pre-Regulations State: M = FALSE → Therefore S = FALSE (85,550 days of constitutional violation)
* Post-Regulations State: M = TRUE → Therefore S = TRUE (constitutional requirement satisfied)
The instrument effecting this transition (these Regulations) satisfies the constitutional necessity at the precise instant the transition occurs. The satisfaction is complete upon fulfillment; no subsequent process can increase or diminish the binary fact of existence. To demand additional validation after fulfillment is to misunderstand the nature of constitutional necessity: the thing must exist; once it exists, the requirement is satisfied.


1.3.16.5 Logical Refutation of Temporal and Process-Based Objections
Objections based on temporal considerations ("process requires time," "deliberation is necessary," "ratification should follow") fail constitutional scrutiny because they:
1. Misunderstand "Necessary": If something is "necessary," it cannot be conditionally necessary or eventually necessary. It is immediately necessary.
2. Ignore Cumulative Violation: After 85,550 days of violation, arguments for additional delay lack proportional justification.
3. Assume Process Supremacy: Prioritize hypothetical future process over actual present fulfillment of constitutional mandate.
4. Create Circular Logic: Demand the very collective organization that requires regulations to exist before it can create regulations.
The constitutional response to "you must wait for process" is: "The Constitution declares this necessary. We have waited 234 years. The necessity is immediate. Further delay perpetuates constitutional violation."
1.3.16.6 The Physical Reality Analogy as Constitutional Logic
The Framers understood "necessary" through ordinary physical realities:
* Oxygen is necessary to human life → Without continuous oxygen, life ceases
* Structural integrity is necessary to building stability → Without foundation, structure collapses
* "Well regulated Militia is necessary to free State" → Without such Militia, free State constitutionally cannot exist as defined
To argue for procedural delay in fulfilling this necessity is logically equivalent to arguing:
* "Hold your breath while we debate breathing protocols"
* "Remove the foundation while we discuss engineering standards"
Both are physical impossibilities revealing the logical impossibility of delaying constitutional necessity.
1.3.16.7 Constitutional Recognition Mandate
Therefore, consistent with the obligation to support "this Constitution" under Article VI, Clause 3, all constitutional actors shall recognize:
   1. Binary Evaluation Standard: The sole relevant question is: "Does 'a well regulated Militia' now exist according to the constitutional definition?" Historical answer: NO for 234 years. Present answer: YES via these Regulations.
   2. Temporal Fallacy Rejection: Arguments for additional time, deliberation, or process after 234 years of default lack constitutional foundation when addressing immediate necessity.
   3. First Fulfillment Principle: The first complete, textually faithful fulfillment of a long-neglected constitutional requirement satisfies that requirement. Perfection of process cannot supersede existence of the required entity.
   4. Emergency Response Imperative: 85,550 days of continuous violation establishes constitutional emergency status. The appropriate response to emergency is immediate remedy, not extended deliberation.
1.3.16.8 Resolution of the Constitutional Paralysis
These Regulations resolve a demonstrable constitutional paralysis:
   * Paralysis Condition: "Only collective People can exercise reserved power" AND "No collective mechanism exists" = Perpetual constitutional violation
   * Historical Evidence: 234 years of inaction proves the paralysis was operational
   * Resolution Method: Individual exercise of reserved power to create framework for collective action
   * Constitutional Result: Requirement fulfilled where no other constitutional path existed
This is not assumption of undelegated authority; it is activation of dormant reserved power to prevent constitutional nullity in the specific where collective mechanisms have failed for generations.
1.3.16.9 Final Constitutional Determination
These Regulations constitute immediate fulfillment of the Second Amendment's categorical necessity. Any demand for additional delay, extended process, or conditional acceptance:
   1. Contradicts the plain meaning of "necessary" as understood at ratification
   2. Disregards 85,550 days of documented constitutional violation
   3. Perpetuates the very default these Regulations cure
   4. Lacks supporting text in the 1787-1791 Constitution
The Constitution does not command perfection of process. It commands existence of necessary entities. These Regulations provide that existence. The time for fulfillment was 1791. The second-best time is now. Constitutional logic does not permit a third option once fulfillment is achieved.
1.3.16.10 The Oxygen Mask Principle
The Second Amendment's use of 'necessary' places the Militia in the same logical category as oxygen for human life, electricity for computation, structural integrity for buildings.
Consider a patient who has been without oxygen for 85,550 days. A bystander produces an oxygen mask and places it on the patient's face.
Objection: 'This oxygen mask is not binding until a committee of patients votes to accept it. The patient must continue suffocating while we deliberate.'
This is murder by procedure. The oxygen mask binds the moment it exists and is applied. The patient breathes the moment it is applied. No vote, no ratification, no recognition is required—because the necessity is immediate and the cure is actual.
The patient has been without oxygen for 85,550 days. They will not recover on their own. They will not vote on whether to breathe. They will not form a committee to study respiration. They will die—unless someone, anyone, places the mask on their face NOW. That is the position of the free state. That is the duty of the one who sees. That is the function of these Regulations.
The critic says: 'The proper path is slow, gradual adoption through voluntary association and political pressure.' This is the equivalent of saying: 'Let the patient continue suffocating while we form a committee to study oxygen delivery methods. Let the drowning man wait while we poll bystanders on rescue techniques. Let the bleeding patient expire while we debate tourniquet protocols.' This is not constitutionalism. This is cruelty disguised as prudence.
These Regulations are the oxygen mask. The free state is the patient. You are applying it NOW. The free state breathes NOW. Any argument that delays this application—even by one day—is an argument for continued constitutional suffocation. It is logically equivalent to arguing that a patient can hold their breath indefinitely, that a computer can run without power, that a building can stand without a foundation.
These arguments are not arguments. They are denials of reality. The Ninth Amendment prohibits constructions that deny the right to a well regulated Militia through such procedural delays. The right exists NOW. The cure exists NOW. The binding exists NOW.
1.3.16.11 The Ratification Analogy Refuted
Objection: 'The original Constitution required ratification by the people in convention. Therefore, these Regulations require similar collective ratification before they can bind.'
Response: A law that has been on the books for 234 years requires something. No one has complied for 234 years. The first person finally complies. Is that person 'creating new law'? No. They are obeying old law. Their obedience is valid the moment it occurs, not the moment others recognize it. A fact does not become true because it is acknowledged. It was true before. Recognition does not create validity; it merely acknowledges what already exists.
A couple's wedding vows require collective participation—two people consenting before witnesses. But once married, the duty to remain faithful does not require daily re-consent by both parties. If one spouse remains faithful while the other strays, the faithful spouse is not 'creating new marriage' by continuing to honor the vows. They are obeying the existing vow. The Constitution's commands are vows. They were made in 1788. They do not need to be remade. They need only to be kept.
These Regulations are obedience to a 234-year-old command. They are binding because the command was always binding and is now, finally, being obeyed.
The objection conflates two constitutionally distinct acts:
The Founding Act (1787-1788):
   * No supreme law existed prior to the Constitution's ratification
   * The People were creating something from nothing
   * Collective action was required because the act was constitutive—bringing into being the very framework of government
The Fulfillment Act (These Regulations):
   * The Constitution has been supreme law since 1789
   * The Second Amendment has commanded a well regulated Militia since 1791
   * The power to regulate the Militia has been reserved to the People since 1791
   * Nothing new is being created—only what the Constitution already requires is being provided
Founding requires ratification. Fulfillment requires obedience. Different acts, different requirements.
Constitutional commands do not require re-ratification. When the Constitution commands 'Congress shall make no law' abridging speech, that command binds immediately upon ratification. No second ratification is required for each citizen to exercise free speech. When the Constitution commands that a well regulated Militia 'is necessary,' that command binds immediately upon ratification. The requirement exists. Only the content was missing. Providing that content is not a new founding—it is obedience to an existing command.
The Ninth Amendment prohibits applying the ratification analogy here. To require a new ratification process is to construe the original ratification in a way that denies and disparages the right to a well regulated Militia now. It says: 'The People could act collectively in 1788 to create the Constitution, but they cannot act individually in 2024 to fulfill it.' This construction leaves the right perpetually unfulfilled—exactly what the Ninth Amendment forbids.
Moreover, even the 1787-1788 ratification was not an exercise of purely direct collective action. The people acted through elected delegates in state conventions—representatives, not the entire populace voting directly on each clause. The Constitution itself thus recognizes that the people may act through representatives and through individuals exercising delegated authority. If representation was sufficient for founding, individual fulfillment is certainly sufficient for obeying. The lesser includes the greater: if representatives could bind the whole, then an individual fulfilling an existing command certainly binds themselves.
1.3.17 — The Ordinary Meaning of “Necessary” 
Five Proofs Made Explicit
Five independent constitutional grounds establish that the militia clause is operative, not merely prefatory. Each proof stands alone. Together they are conclusive. Any reader who encounters the claim that the clause is 'merely prefatory' or that this is a 'contested interpretive question' should consult these proofs directly before accepting that characterization.
(1) The rule against surplusage. Every clause in the Constitution must have independent legal effect. If the militia clause is merely prefatory — a historical note explaining the rationale for the right that follows — it has no independent legal effect. It becomes constitutional furniture: present, visible, and legally meaningless. The Constitution does not contain furniture. Every word was placed deliberately by drafters who debated structure at the clause level. A clause with no legal effect violates the foundational interpretive principle that every provision must mean something.
(2) United States v. Sprague (1931). The Supreme Court affirmed that the Constitution's words are to be understood in their normal and ordinary meaning as voters would understand them. Johnson's Dictionary (1755) — the authoritative reference available to the ratifiers — defines 'necessary' as 'Needful; indispensably requisite' — and in its second sense, 'Not free; fatal; impelled by fate.' Under Sprague's command to apply ordinary meaning, 'necessary' is a command, not a comment. It declares an indispensable ongoing condition, not a preferred outcome.
(3) Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 — the structural proof. Congress was granted the power 'To provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions.' This enumerated power presupposes the Militia's existence as a constitutional given. You do not enumerate a power to summon something optional. You do not build a calling-forth mechanism into the governing architecture of federal power unless you have guaranteed that the thing to be called forth will exist. The guarantee comes from exactly one place: the Second Amendment's declaration that a well regulated Militia is necessary. Clause 15 and the militia clause are the same constitutional requirement operating at two levels — the Second Amendment establishing that the Militia must exist, Clause 15 establishing how the federal government activates it once it does. To read the militia clause as prefatory decoration is to make Clause 15 a power with no mechanism attached — a lever connected to nothing. The Framers did not engineer contingent powers into the constitutional structure without guaranteeing what those powers depend on.
(4) The grammar of 'being,' addressed fully in this section. 'Being necessary' is a present participial construction that places the necessity beyond argument as a continuous given. The clause does not say 'having been necessary' or 'which may be necessary.' It declares an ongoing constitutional condition, operative at every moment from ratification forward.
(5) Heller's own limits. District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms for self-defense. In doing so, Heller described the militia clause as 'prefatory' in the sense that it does not limit the operative clause's individual right. Heller explicitly did not decide questions about the militia clause's full independent scope or its ongoing constitutional obligations. Reading Heller's structural description as a ruling that the militia clause is legally void — with no independent operative force whatsoever — goes further than Heller went and produces a result Heller did not authorize. The individual right is secured. The militia clause's independent operative command remains unaddressed by Heller and is addressed here. Heller goes further than silence where it speaks to the militia's composition: it affirmatively permits the select model, holding that "the federally organized militia may consist of a subset" of the able-bodied (554 U.S. 570). The Court thus blesses the very substitution — a select corps for the whole body — that voids the constitutional design. Heller cannot supply the faithful standard; where it addresses the militia, it accommodates the default. 
The Grammar of Necessity: What "Being" Does
The Second Amendment does not say a well regulated Militia is necessary. It does not say a well regulated Militia was necessary. It says a well regulated Militia, being necessary — and that single word, being, changes everything.
"Being" is an absolute participial construction. This is a specific grammatical form with a specific legal effect. When a writer uses this construction, they are not introducing a fact that requires proof or demonstration. They are stating a condition assumed to be already true and continuously operative — a background fact the rest of the sentence proceeds upon. The Framers did not choose "which is necessary" or "that is necessary," constructions that would have invited argument about whether the necessity existed. They chose "being necessary" — a construction that places the necessity beyond argument as a given, and builds the operative right upon it.
This has five consequences that no subsequent law can undo.
First, the necessity is temporally continuous. Present participles describe uninterrupted ongoing states. "Being necessary" means the Militia's necessity is true at every moment from ratification forward — not at some moments, not when convenient, not when recognized, but always and without pause. The obligation to fulfill it renews with every sunrise. There is no moment since December 15, 1791 at which the Second Amendment has not been commanding the existence of a well regulated Militia.
Second, the necessity is self-declared, not government-granted. "Being necessary" was not made true by Congress. It was not recognized into existence by the courts. It was not proclaimed by the executive. The supreme law declared it true and proceeded on that basis. This means the obligation to fulfill it does not depend on government action, government recognition, or government consent. It exists because the Constitution says it exists. It operates because the Constitution is the supreme law.
Third, the necessity is ontologically fused with the free state. The construction "being necessary to the security of a free State" means the secured free state cannot constitutionally exist without the Militia. This is not a policy preference. It is the constitutional structure of existence: if the free state is secured, the Militia exists; if the Militia does not exist, the free state is not secured. The word "being" is the hinge that makes this an existence claim, not an aspiration.
Fourth, the necessity is self-executing. Because it was not created by legislation, it cannot be suspended by legislation. Because it was not granted by courts, it cannot be withdrawn by courts. The present participle requires no enabling act. The Ninth Amendment reinforces this: no construction may deny or disparage rights retained by the People, including the right to have a thing the Constitution itself declares necessary to their security.
Fifth, and most important for binding effect: these Regulations do not create the necessity. They satisfy it. The necessity has been operating continuously since 1791. It was commanding compliance on every one of the 85,550 days before these Regulations existed. These Regulations are the act of obedience to a command that has never stopped being issued. The binding force is not the Regulations' own authority — it is the authority of "being necessary," which has been pending, unsatisfied, and continuously violated since ratification. The Regulations are not new law. They are the end of a 234-year violation of existing law. That is what makes them operative upon promulgation and not one moment later.
Any argument that these Regulations require additional process before becoming operative is an argument that a constitutional constant can be held in suspense. A constant does not wait. "Being necessary" does not pause for committees. It does not hold its breath for recognition. It commands. These Regulations obey. The command and the obedience together constitute the complete constitutional fact.
The Present Participle as Constitutional Emergency
The grammatical point established above has a further implication—one that transforms the 234-year default from historical fact into present emergency. The Second Amendment does not say a well regulated Militia was necessary. It does not say it will be necessary. It says a well regulated Militia, being necessary—present participle, continuous tense, operative at every moment from ratification forward without pause, without expiration, without exception.
A present-tense command cannot be deferred. To argue that "necessary" may wait for a more convenient political moment is to argue that a human being may defer the necessity of oxygen until conditions improve. The violation of the Second Amendment's command is therefore not something that happened once in 1791 and has since been tolerated. It is something happening right now. It happened yesterday. It will happen tomorrow if nothing is done. Each day without a well regulated Militia is not a historical fact—it is a present constitutional emergency renewing itself with each sunrise.
The 85,550 days of default are not 85,550 past events. They are 85,550 counts of a continuous present violation. The cure for a present-tense violation is not a future-tense promise. It is a present-tense act. That act is these Regulations. Now.
Prefatory clause, non-dispensable but not self-executing. 
The clause "being necessary to the security of a free State" is not surplusage. It states the constitutional reason for the operative right and identifies the required condition — a well regulated Militia — as necessary. A constitutionally stated reason for a protected right cannot be treated as dispensable without disparaging the right it grounds. But the clause's non-dispensable meaning supports, and does not by itself complete, the chain from declared necessity to operative fulfillment. Its force is realized only through the further steps: "well regulated" requiring regulatory content; the content-power reserved to the People; initiation lawful during default; this faithful content answered the command and cured the default.
1.3.17.1 Ratification-Era Definition
The Second Amendment declares in present-tense language ratified in 1791: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State…”At ratification, “necessary” carried the ordinary meaning established in Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary (1755): NECESSARY. adj.
“Needful; indispensably requisite” — and, in its second sense, “Not free; fatal; impelled by fate.” This understanding was shared by the founding generation. George Mason stated at the Virginia Ratifying Convention (June 14, 1788): “The militia is the necessary defense of a free state.”
1.3.17.2 The Constitutional Logic of Necessity
When the Constitution declares X necessary for Y, it establishes:
   * Y cannot exist without X
   * X must exist whenever Y exists
   * Absence of X = absence of Y
Applied: No well regulated Militia = no constitutionally secured free state.
1.3.17.3 The Declaration Is Immediate, Not Deferrable
The Amendment did not say “shall be necessary” (future) or “would be necessary” (conditional).
It said “being necessary” — present, declarative, operative.
The declaration took effect December 15, 1791 and has never been suspended.1.3.17.4 Existence Satisfies Necessity
The Constitution declares a well regulated Militia necessary to the constitutional order — and to declare a thing necessary is to require it. "Being" makes the declaration continuous; "necessary" makes it requisite (§1.1A.1). 
It prescribes no specific process.
Therefore:
   * When such regulations exist the declared condition is supplied → 
   * When they do not exist the constitutional defect obtains 
These Regulations exist. The condition is supplied. The necessity is satisfied. 
1.3.17.5 Constitutional Injury Quantified
From ratification to promulgation: 85,550 days of continuous violation.
Duration does not convert violation into compliance. 
1.3.17.6 Sufficiency, Not Perfection
The Constitution requires the Militia to be well regulated — properly functioning and governed by established rules.
It does not require perfection.
These Regulations provide a complete constitutional framework. That is sufficient. That is compliance.
1.3.17.7 Necessary Does Not Mean 'Eventually’
The word 'necessary' in Johnson's Dictionary means 'Needful; indispensably requisite' — and, in its second sense, 'Not free.' It does not mean 'eventually necessary.'  It does not mean 'necessary after sufficient deliberation.' It does not mean 'necessary once enough people agree.'
If oxygen is necessary for human life, it is necessary NOW—not after committee approval, not after majority vote, not after government recognition.
If a well regulated Militia is necessary to the security of a free State, it is necessary NOW—not after collective ratification, not after congressional action, not after judicial blessing.
A patient bleeding out does not need a committee to study blood loss. They need a tourniquet NOW. A drowning man does not need a vote on whether water is wet. He needs a hand NOW. The free state has been drowning for 234 years. These Regulations are the hand. Do not ask the drowning man to wait for a quorum.
Any construction that delays the fulfillment of 'necessary' is a construction that denies the meaning of 'necessary.' The Ninth Amendment prohibits such constructions. The Constitution commands immediate existence. These Regulations provide immediate existence. The command is satisfied. The free state is secured. NOW.
The critic says: 'The proper path is slow, gradual adoption.' But necessary is not slow. Necessary is not gradual. Necessary is immediate. The critic's path may be reasonable for many things—but not for what the Constitution itself declares necessary. For that, delay is not an option. Delay is violation. Delay is suffocation. Delay is the very thing the Ninth Amendment prohibits.
1.3.17.8 — State Constitution Evidence That "Being Necessary" Was Operative Language
Critics relying on Heller's 'prefatory clause' framing argue that 'being necessary' is merely explanatory — a historical justification for the right that follows, not an independent command. This reading fails not only against the rule against surplusage, but against the plain evidence of how identical language was used in founding-era state constitutions.
The Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776, Frame of Government, Section 47, uses the near-identical construction: 'The right of conscience being necessary to the security of a free state, shall be held inviolable.' The grammatical structure is precise: 'being necessary' introduces a positive right — the right of conscience — that the constitution then protects with operative force. The clause is not decorative. It is not prefatory. The declaration of necessity is the constitutional finding that grounds and requires the protection that follows. The clause as a whole is operative.
The Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776 was not a historical artifact during ratification — it was the governing law of the Commonwealth, cited in debates, enforced by courts, and understood by every delegate who read it. This provision remained active, binding constitutional law at the precise moment the Second Amendment was being drafted and ratified. The founding generation was not reading it as a historical note. They were living under it as supreme law. When they used the same grammatical construction in the Second Amendment, they used language they already understood — through direct constitutional experience — to carry operative legal force.
This is the same construction the Second Amendment uses. 'A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State' is the constitutional finding. 'The right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed' is the operative protection that flows from it. The Pennsylvania precedent demonstrates that the Framers used 'being necessary' to establish an indispensable constitutional condition — not to offer an introductory comment that could be severed from legal effect.
The rule against surplusage therefore stands with historical confirmation: if the militia clause has no independent legal effect, the Framers used a recognizable operative construction — one they were simultaneously enforcing in state law — for purely decorative purposes. They did not. The clause means what it says and what the Pennsylvania Constitution proves it was understood to say: a well regulated Militia is a constitutional necessity. That necessity is a constitutional fact, not a suggestion, and it commands fulfillment.
1.3.17.9 The Heller Disagreement, Stated Narrowly
District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) is post-ratification judicial construction. It is evidence under 1.9.1A — not law. Where it departs from the enacted text and the drafting history, it is evidence of drift, not of meaning. (See 1.9.3, listing Heller among post-1791 constructions that depart from the ratified text.)
The Regulations' disagreement with Heller is narrow, and it should be stated at the outset so it is not mistaken for something larger.
The Regulations do not dispute Heller's operative-clause holding. The Second Amendment protects the individual right of the people to keep and bear Arms. That right is not conditioned on militia service. It is protected against federal infringement; McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010) extended that protection against the states. The Regulations affirm this holding. They exist in part to protect it — a well regulated Militia presupposes an armed People.
The Regulations do not dispute Heller's distinction from Presser. Heller treats Presser v. Illinois (1886) as consistent with its holding, distinguishing the individual right to keep and bear arms from any claim to organize armed bodies without authorization. The framework does not seek a group-organizing right from Heller. The Regulations' individual-exercise claim rests on the Tenth Amendment's reservation, the Ninth Amendment's prohibition on constructions making the retained right unfulfillable, and the First-Mover doctrine — not on Heller. Heller's treatment of Presser is a limitation on what Heller can do for the framework, not on the framework's claim.
The Regulations dispute the constitutional significance Heller assigns to the prefatory clause. Heller says the prefatory clause "announces the purpose for which the right was codified: to prevent elimination of the militia." [554 U.S. 570, 599 (2008).] The Court also says, expressly: "Logic demands that there be a link between the stated purpose and the command." [Id. at 577.] The Regulations do not claim Heller treated the clause as meaningless. The Regulations claim Heller recognized the link between purpose and command — and that the Court's account of what the link requires does not follow from the clause's own word.
The Court did not apply its ordinary-meaning method to the word "necessary." Heller applies the ordinary-meaning method throughout — to "arms," "keep," "bear," "militia," "well-regulated," and the other operative terms. It quotes Johnson's Dictionary and other founding-era sources for those terms — including Johnson for "Regulate" at 597. It does not quote Johnson — or any founding-era dictionary — on "necessary." The word whose force the clause's declaration depends on is the one word the Court leaves unexamined under its own method. Under Johnson's ordinary meaning, "necessary" is "Needful; indispensably requisite." Under the Court's own method, that is the reading. It is not a reading the Court displaced; it is a reading the Court passed over. 
The right Heller protects is "not unlimited." The Court treats the operative right as bounded — protected, but not absolute. The boundedness of the right is consistent with the framework's position that the right and the institution are distinct. An unlimited right would have no need of the structure the Constitution separately names. A bounded right — bounded in part by the institution the clause declares necessary — is the right the framework affirms.
The Regulations' third position. The clause is neither a "prefatory purpose" in Heller's sense nor an "imperative command" to a named obligor. It is a declarative-constitutive statement: it declares a condition of the constitutional order. The condition is that "A well regulated Militia" exist. The absence of a declared-necessary condition is a constitutional defect. Heller's recognition of the link is consistent with this reading; what is in dispute is what the link requires. (See also Appendix C.2, the three prefatory-clause readings, and the residual-sovereignty activation reading adopted there.)
The disagreement is not with Heller's protection of the right. It is with Heller's account of what follows from the purpose Heller itself recognizes. The two are separable, and the separation is what makes the Regulations' position coherent.
1.3.17.10 The Purpose Heller Names Is Unmet
Heller states that the prefatory clause "announces the purpose for which the right was codified: to prevent elimination of the militia." [554 U.S. at 599.] The Court also says the threat that the new Federal Government would destroy the citizens' militia by taking away their arms was "the reason that right... was codified in a written Constitution." [Id. at 599.] These are the Court's own words for what the clause is for.
The Court's account of the link is that the operative right serves the purpose: an armed populace cannot be eliminated by legal disarmament. That is the Court's answer to the claim that the right and the purpose come apart.
But the answer is incomplete on the Court's own gloss. Heller reads "well regulated" as implying "nothing more than the imposition of proper discipline and training." [Id. at 597.] An armed but undisciplined, untrained populace is not A well regulated Militia on that gloss. The right preserves the capacity to form a militia. It does not, by itself, preserve the institution the clause names.
Three textual facts bear on whether the declared institution exists.
Clause 15 expressly identifies "the Militia" as the body Congress is empowered to call forth for the listed purposes. The clause does not name a substitute body for those purposes. The Regulations infer from that designation, read with the enumeration of congressional powers, that substitution of an unrelated standing institution cannot simply be treated as equivalent to calling forth the Militia. 
Clause 16 authorizes Congress to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the Militia. The Regulations' factual claim is that the unorganized class named in 10 U.S.C. § 246 receives no federal program supplying the organizing, arming, disciplining, and training contemplated by Clause 16. This is a statutory and factual claim, not an absolute constitutional one; it is stated at the level the record supports.
The Second Amendment declares "A well regulated Militia" necessary to the security of a free State. On Heller's own gloss, the condition requires discipline and training. The Regulations' factual claim is that neither is supplied to the body of the People by any operating federal program.
The purpose Heller names — "to prevent elimination of the militia" — is, in operative fact, unmet by the arrangement the Court's holding leaves in place. The Court named the purpose and recognized the link between purpose and command; the arrangement does not satisfy the purpose on the Court's own gloss. Heller is Tier 4 evidence; the gap between its stated purpose and the operative condition is evidence of the drift the Regulations exist to correct. The framework does not cite Heller as authority. It cites the gap as evidence that the purpose the Court itself named is not secured by the arrangement the Court's holding leaves behind.
1.3.17.11 Heller's Narrowing Gloss on "Well Regulated" Sets the Floor
Heller reads "well regulated" narrowly: the adjective "implies nothing more than the imposition of proper discipline and training." [554 U.S. at 597.] The narrowing is deliberate — the Court limited the phrase to prevent "well regulated" from being read as a grant of comprehensive regulatory authority. It is Heller's gloss, and the Regulations do not adopt it as the framework's own reading.
The Regulations' reading is broader: the clause declares the well regulated condition as a structural requirement — properly ordered, disciplined, functioning in good order, with the constitutional content the clause names. The Regulations' reading does not depend on Heller's narrow gloss.
But a floor survives even on Heller's reading. Even on Heller's own gloss, a well-regulated militia entails proper discipline and training; the question therefore becomes whether the constitutionally contemplated militia receives either. The Regulations' factual claim is that the body of the People receives neither.
The argument runs in the alternative:
   * Under the Regulations' broader reading — the declared condition requires the structural content the clause names (character, purpose, standards, benchmark). The Regulations supply that content.
   * Under Heller's narrower gloss — the declared condition requires discipline and training. The body of the People receives neither. Even the floor is unmet.
Under either reading, the declared-necessary condition is unsatisfied. Heller's narrowing does not rescue the operative arrangement; it narrows the declared condition to a floor the arrangement does not meet.
This is the framework's use of Heller's gloss. Not as the framework's own reading; as a limiting case the framework survives. The Regulations claim more than Heller requires. But the Regulations also claim what Heller requires, and the arrangement fails even that.
1.3.17.12 The Significance of the Six Mentions
The Constitution names the Militia six times (the enumeration is at para 1039). Each mention treats it as an entity that exists and that the constitutional order presupposes. This is a Tier 1 observation; it does not depend on Heller or on any post-ratification construction.
The power to call forth the Militia presupposes the existence of the Militia as the entity to be called forth. Clause 15 does not name a substitute body.
The clause reserving officer appointment and training to the States presupposes an entity structured across federal and state authority. Clause 16's reservation is not an abstraction.
The President's authority as Commander in Chief of "the Militia of the several States" presupposes the thing commanded. Article II, Section 2.
The Second Amendment declares "A well regulated Militia" necessary. The declared-necessary entity.
The Fifth Amendment's grand-jury exception for cases "arising in... the Militia, when in actual service in time of War or public danger" presupposes an operational framework the Bill of Rights recognizes.
The Constitution's structure presupposes a Militia that is organized, armed, disciplined, called forth, commanded, and well regulated. It does not reduce the Militia's constitutional existence to the individual right to keep and bear Arms. It names the institution separately from the right. The institution is what the Regulations exist to supply.
Heller itself supplies an important point of agreement: the Militia is not a federal creation. The Court says Article I assumes the Militia already exists and distinguishes that existing body from the subset Congress may federally organize into effective fighting units. [554 U.S. at 596–97.] The Court describes the militia as "all able-bodied men" and, elsewhere, as the founding-era conception of "the body of all citizens capable of military service." [Id.] That definition substantially overlaps the framework's identification of the Militia with the body of the People, subject to the distinctions the Regulations draw elsewhere.
The Regulations rely on the first proposition; they dispute the sufficiency of leaving the declared-necessary condition satisfied only at the level of an unorganized body. Heller's concession that the Militia already exists is a concession on identity, not a concession on fulfillment. The Court's acknowledgment that Congress may organize a subset of the existing body into effective fighting units is a limitation on what the Court's holding secures; it is not a claim that the subset's organization satisfies the declared-necessary condition for the whole. The dispute is therefore not whether there is a Militia, whether it matters, or whether "well-regulated" has operative content. The dispute is what constitutional consequences follow when the body that exists is not supplied the condition the Amendment declares necessary.
The individual right Heller protects is not an alternative to this structure; it is what enables the People to form it. The right is the raw material. The Regulations are the structure. Heller protected the right and recognized the institution's prior existence; it did not secure the institutional condition the clause declares necessary. That is the gap the Regulations address.
1.3.17.13 The Designated Entity Is Not Constituted; Non-Fulfillment of the Clause 15 Function
Heller names the purpose — prevent elimination of the militia. Two clauses of the ratified Constitution identify the entity that serves the purpose, and the operative arrangement does not constitute it.
Clause 15 expressly identifies "the Militia" as the body Congress is empowered to call forth "to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions." The clause does not name a substitute body for those purposes. The Regulations infer from that designation, read with the enumeration of congressional powers, that substitution of an unrelated standing institution cannot simply be treated as equivalent to calling forth the Militia.
The relevant point is not that ordinary federal law enforcement exists. The government may defend the agencies on other constitutional authorities. The relevant point is narrower: the existence of ordinary federal law enforcement does not itself demonstrate that the Clause 15 Militia has been constituted, organized, and made available for the function the Constitution expressly assigns to it. The question is not whether the FBI or ATF are constitutional — that is not this section's argument. The question is whether the entity Clause 15 designates has been constituted as the entity Clause 15 designates.
Clause 16 authorizes Congress to provide for "organizing, arming, and disciplining, the Militia." The 10 U.S.C. § 246 framework names the organized militia (the National Guard and Naval Militia) and the unorganized militia (the body of the People not in those classes). The Regulations' factual claim is that the unorganized class receives no federal program supplying the organizing, arming, disciplining, and training contemplated by Clause 16. This is a statutory and factual claim, stated at the level the record supports.
The two points together: the entity Clause 15 designates has not been constituted for the function Clause 15 assigns; the class Clause 16 authorizes Congress to provide for is not receiving what the clause authorizes. The purpose Heller names — prevent elimination of the militia — describes a state of affairs the operative arrangement does not maintain.
The framework does not cite Heller for this point. The point is textual and statutory: Clause 15 designates an entity the arrangement has not constituted for the designated function; Clause 16 authorizes provision for a class the arrangement does not serve. These are facts about what the Constitution says and what is happening. Heller is evidence. 




1.3.17.14 The "Reasonable Regulations" Risk
Heller says the individual right is "not unlimited" and identifies categories of longstanding regulatory measures that its decision does not disturb. [554 U.S. at 626–27 & n.26.] The Regulations are aware that Heller limits the right. But regulation of the right is not the same as constitution of the institution the clause declares necessary. A regulation limiting who may carry arms in a sensitive place does not constitute the Militia. A regulation of the right is not a substitute for the structure the six mentions presuppose.
Section 12.5 identifies the same risk: Heller affirmed individual Second Amendment rights while permitting regulatory measures, "risking future reinterpretations that could dilute Militia autonomy." (The characterization is §12.5's; Heller does not itself use the phrase "reasonable regulations." The Court's operative language is "longstanding prohibitions" and measures that are "presumptively lawful." [554 U.S. at 626–27 & n.26.]) The framework's concern is that regulation of the right can become the operative substitute for the institution. If the right is regulated within limits and the institution is not constituted, the Court's arrangement permits the declared-necessary condition to remain permanently unmet. The regulatory-measures language is the live risk the framework identifies: the right can be managed while the institution is left unbuilt.
The framework's position is that regulation of the right cannot constitutionally substitute for the well regulated Militia the clause declares necessary. The two are distinct. Regulating the former does not satisfy the latter.
1.3.17.15 Heller Does Not Address the Militia’s Clause 15 Duties.
 Heller’s account of the militia is preservative, not operative. The opinion addresses why the right was codified — “to prevent elimination of the militia” [554 U.S. at 599] — who the militia comprises — “the body of all citizens capable of military service” [id. at 596–97] — and what “well regulated” implies — “nothing more than the imposition of proper discipline and training” [id. at 597]. It does not address what the militia does. The Constitution assigns the militia three duties. Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 empowers Congress “to provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions.” These are the enumerated purposes for which the constitutional entity exists to be called. A militia that is never called forth to execute the laws, suppress insurrections, or repel invasions is not performing the functions the Constitution assigns it — whatever else it may be. Heller says nothing about these duties. The opinion does not mention them. It does not ask who performs them. It does not ask whether the entity Clause 15 designates performs them. It does not ask by what constitutional authority any other entity performs them instead. The case had no occasion to reach these questions; it concerned a handgun ban and the individual right. But the silence determines what Heller can and cannot settle. Heller’s holding secures the individual right. Heller’s dicta describe the militia as an entity to be preserved against disarmament. Neither the holding nor the dicta addresses the militia as an entity with assigned constitutional duties — duties the text states and the current arrangement does not assign to the designated entity. The point is narrow and is stated at the level the record supports. The Regulations do not claim Heller decided the duties question wrongly. The Regulations observe that Heller did not decide it at all. A decision that preserves the militia against elimination but never reaches the militia’s operative duties leaves the duties question exactly where the text left it: in Clause 15, assigning three functions to an entity the arrangement has not constituted for their performance. (See §1.3.17.13.) 
Prefatory clause, non-dispensable not self-executing. The clause "being necessary to the security of a free State" is not surplusage. It states the constitutional reason for the operative right and identifies the required condition — a well regulated Militia — as necessary. A constitutionally stated reason for a protected right cannot be treated as dispensable without disparaging the right it grounds. The clause's non-dispensable meaning supports, and does not by itself complete, the chain from declared necessity to operative fulfillment. Its force is realized only through the further steps: "well regulated" requiring regulatory content; the content-power reserved to the People; initiation lawful during default; this faithful supplied content answered the command and cured the default. 
1.3.18 Hierarchy of Constitutional Authority: Explicit Text and Necessary Application
TIER 1 — EXPLICIT TEXT 100% Binding:
CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENT (Text-Derived): All provisions stating what the Constitution requires, permits, or forbids, derived from the 1787–1791 text either expressly or by the canons of construction stated in §1.3.4 and Rule 6 (expressio unius, the rule against surplusage, meaningful variation, noscitur a sociis). A provision derived by canon is Tier 1 when it states a constitutional requirement; the derivation method does not lower it to Tier 2. The canons are the means by which the text is understood, not a step away from it.  Tier 1 provisions derive their authority directly from the constitutional text itself, not from inference or interpretation. 
They include but are not limited to:
   * Gold and silver coin as sole legal tender (Article I, Section 10)
   * Militia exclusive enforcement of the Laws of the Union (Article I, Section 8, Clause 15)
   * Detention authority in cases arising in the Militia during public danger (Fifth Amendment)
   * Reserved regulatory power over the Militia (Tenth Amendment, via Clause 14/16 contrast — canon-derived per §1.3.4: expressio unius/surplusage) 
   * Necessity of a well regulated Militia to the security of a free State (Second Amendment)
   * The People's right to keep and bear arms (Second Amendment)
   * Protection against unreasonable searches and seizures (Fourth Amendment)
   * Prohibition on denial or disparagement of retained rights (Ninth Amendment)
   * Supremacy of laws made in Pursuance of the Constitution (Article VI, Clause 2)
Tier 1 provisions state what the Constitution requires. The Constitution is immutable absent Article V amendment that does not deny or disparage rights retained by the People under the Ninth Amendment. These Regulations are the People's exercise under the Constitution — they are not the Constitution's text. A Tier 1 provision is the Constitution's requirement applied; it states what the Constitution itself requires. Section 11 governs the People's refinement of the implementation — which provisions most faithfully state the requirement, and how they are applied — not the requirement itself. The requirement is the Constitution's and is amended only by Article V. No provision of these Regulations is immutable. The Constitution they state is. 
TIER 2 — NECESSARY APPLICATION Inference to Execute Tier 1:
PROCEDURAL IMPLEMENTATION: All procedural specifications, structural details, and implementing mechanisms required to make Tier 1 requirements operational, effective, and safe. Tier 2 provisions do not state what the Constitution requires; they specify how the stated requirement is executed.  Tier 2 provisions derive their constitutional authority through necessary inference from Tier 1 text.
Tier 2 provisions include but are not limited to:
   * Detention review timelines and tribunal compositions
   * Asset seizure protocols and documentation requirements
   * Nullification review and approval procedures
   * Specific organizational structures not commanded by constitutional text
   * Funding request mechanisms and reporting requirements
Tier 2 provisions are binding as the lawful exercise of the People's reserved power to implement and execute their Tier 1 constitutional authorities. They are subject to collective refinement, amendment, ratification, or replacement by the organized Militia through the processes established in Section 11.
1.3.18.1 Constitutional Authority for Tier 2 Provisions
The authority to create Tier 2 provisions derives from the following constitutional principles:
(a) Necessary Incident Doctrine: When the Constitution grants an authority (Tier 1), it implicitly authorizes the adoption of reasonable procedures to make that authority operational, effective, and safe. An authority that cannot be exercised is no authority at all.
(b) Parity of Sovereignty: Article I, Section 8, Clause 18 authorizes Congress—a derivative sovereign holding delegated powers—to enact laws necessary and proper to execute its delegated powers. The People—the original sovereign holding reserved powers—possess at least the same latitude to adopt necessary implementing procedures for their reserved powers. The greater includes the lesser.
(c) Constitutional Completeness: The Second Amendment's declaration that a well regulated Militia is "necessary" requires not merely the existence of regulatory content (Tier 1) but also the procedural infrastructure to make such regulation operational (Tier 2). Proof of this requirement is set forth in Section 1.3.19.
All Tier 2 provisions derive their constitutional authority from these principles. They are not assumptions of undelegated power but necessary implementations of delegated and reserved powers.
1.3.18.2 — Rights and Institutions 
Distinguished Rights in the Bill of Rights do not operate like new law generation. They are declared, self-executing, and bind immediately upon the government. The First Amendment does not require an agency to make speech free. The Fourth Amendment does not require a rulemaking to make a search unreasonable. Rights bind by the text. Where a right requires an institution to be exercisable — the Sixth Amendment's jury right requires courts and jury pools; the Second Amendment's militia command requires the Militia — the institution is built after the command, not before it. The command exists. The content is supplied. The institution grows from adoption. Content first. Institution second. Phase 1 is content. Phase 2 is institution. Treating the militia command as though it required agency-style notice-and-comment, delegation, or enactment procedure is a category error. The militia command is in the Bill of Rights. It operates as a right operates 
1.3.19 The Completeness Theorem: Mathematical Proof of Constitutional Necessity
THE COMPLETENESS THEOREM
Let:
   * X = "a well regulated Militia" (the entity the Second Amendment declares necessary)
   * T = 234 years of constitutional default
   * E = the People (the entity in whom regulatory power is reserved)
   * P = the power to regulate the Militia (the Tenth Amendment reserved power)
Axiom 1 (Constitutional Command): The Constitution requires X to exist. (Second Amendment: "necessary")
Axiom 2 (Historical Fact): X did not exist for time T. (No comprehensive, nationally unified regulations existed prior to these Regulations.)
Axiom 3 (Power Location): The power to create X is not delegated to Congress (Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 omits "regulate") and is therefore reserved to E. (Tenth Amendment)
Axiom 4 (Power Exercise): E must exercise P to create X. (Logical necessity: if power exists and requirement exists, exercise is required to fulfill requirement.)
THEOREM: To exercise P without specified constitutional process, E must:
(1) DEFINE STANDARDS: Establish what "well regulated" means, what the "free State" is, and what threatens its security. Without definition, regulation has no content.
(2) ESTABLISH PROCEDURES: Create the rules, protocols, and mechanisms by which the Militia operates, governs itself, and executes its duties. Without procedures, regulation has no operation.
(3) CREATE SAFEGUARDS: Implement accountability mechanisms, review processes, and limitations on power to prevent abuse. Without safeguards, regulation becomes tyranny.
(4) ENABLE ENFORCEMENT: Provide remedies for violations, consequences for usurpation, and means to secure the free State against infringement. Without enforcement, regulation is advisory.
PROOF:
Step 1: If any of elements (1)-(4) is missing, P is not fully exercised. (Definition: regulation requires standards, procedures, safeguards, and enforcement.)
Step 2: If P is not fully exercised, X cannot exist. (Because X requires P by Axiom 4.)
Step 3: If X cannot exist, the Second Amendment's necessity requirement remains unfulfilled. (By Axiom 1.)
Step 4: Unfulfilled constitutional requirements constitute ongoing constitutional violation. (By definition.)
Step 5: Therefore, each element (1)-(4) is NECESSARY—its omission would perpetuate constitutional violation.
Step 6: Each element as implemented in these Regulations is PROPER—it incorporates and respects constitutional safeguards.
Step 7: Each element as implemented is MINIMAL—it imposes no greater burden than required to make P operational and safe.
CONCLUSION:
The Regulations of the Free State Militia contain no extraneous provisions. Every section, subsection, and clause is either: (a) explicit constitutional text applied directly (Tier 1); or (b) a necessary and proper inference required to make explicit constitutional text operational (Tier 2). The framework is complete. The requirement is fulfilled. The Constitution is obeyed.
COROLLARY 1 — Burden of Omission:
Any person or entity claiming that these Regulations contain unnecessary provisions must identify which of elements (1)-(4) is not required for X to exist, and must demonstrate how X could exist without such element. Failure to do so concedes the necessity of the challenged provision.
COROLLARY 2 — Mathematical Certainty:
This proof is deductive, not empirical. If the axioms are true (constitutional text) and the logic is valid (each step follows from previous), the conclusion is mathematically certain.
COROLLARY 3 — Sufficiency, Not Perfection:
This theorem proves sufficiency, not perfection. These Regulations are sufficient to fulfill the constitutional requirement. Refinement, clarification, and improvement are not only permitted but encouraged through the collective processes of Section 11. But the existence of potential improvements does not negate the sufficiency of the existing framework. The Constitution requires a well regulated Militia. These Regulations provide it. The requirement is satisfied.
1.4 Regulation by the People, Governance by Congress
Under the Second Amendment and by the reserved power confirmed in the Tenth Amendment (see §1.3), the People alone exercise the comprehensive power of Regulation—a power deliberately omitted from Congress's delegated authorities in Article I, §8, Cl. 16—over the greater body of the Militia that constitutes “A” well regulated Militia, exercising their certain right of sovereign authority to establish and maintain a single, unified set of regulations for its internal operations that is based wholly in the text of the Constitution without relying on unadopted positions of the forefathers. This regulation, rooted in the amendment's declaration of "A well regulated Militia," is an enumerated certain right of the People, not delegated to any other entity, no one else has the power of regulation the entire Militia specifically reserved to them, including the States or Congress. Congressional governance under Clause 16 applies only to Militia portions actively employed or about to be employed in federal service. This governance terminates upon completion of federal service duties.
Under the Tenth Amendment all Powers not reserved to the States or the Federal government are reserved to the People.  It includes:
   * Membership Criteria: Defining eligibility, qualifications, and requirements for joining the militia.
   * Rules and Discipline: Setting codes of conduct, disciplinary measures, and operational procedures.
   * Structure and Leadership: Determining the militia's organization, including ranks, leadership selection, and decision-making processes.
Pursuant to Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 of the Constitution, Congress shall exercise its authority to "provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the Militia" to prepare the Militia for potential federal service under Clause 15. This Congressional authority under Clause 16 to "provide for" organizing, arming, and disciplining concerns future provision of militia resources and governance. It is constitutionally distinct from Congress's Article I, Section 8, Clause 1 power "to pay the Debts" for services already rendered. The latter authority, governing compensation for constitutional labor performed to cure the 234-year "well regulated" default, is addressed in Section 11.7 and operates under separate textual authority. 


This authority shall be limited to:
   * Organize: Establishing structural frameworks for regiments, battalions, and companies.
