It conditions supremacy on pursuance — all law-making, including amendments, must conform to the Constitution's existing commands to claim the status of supreme Law. The Ninth Amendment resolves internal conflicts: no construction shall deny or disparage rights retained by the People. Together, these three provisions protect the Constitution's substantive core against amendments that would subvert it — not by voiding Article V, but by conditioning the supremacy of its products on conformity with the foundational commands the People built into the text at ratification. The People, in ratifying these clauses, built the rule of resolution into the Constitution itself.
1.9.10.2 — The Supremacy Clause as Affirmative Foundation
The Plain Text:
The Supremacy Clause (Article VI, Clause 2) establishes three categories of supreme Law:
This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land.
These Regulations are supreme Law under each of the three analyses below — the analyses applicable to an instrument that is not a treaty and claims nothing under that category. Each stands independently. Together they are conclusive. 
Analysis One — "This Constitution":
The Second Amendment is part of "This Constitution." It declares a well regulated Militia necessary to the security of a free State. That declaration is already supreme Law — not because these Regulations exist, but because the Constitution itself commands it. These Regulations fulfill that command. Their authority derives from the command's supremacy, not from any independent claim. The Second Amendment's necessity command was supreme Law on the day of ratification. It remains supreme Law today. These Regulations are the instrument of its fulfillment. The fulfillment carries the command’s supremacy into operation — not as an addition to “This Constitution,” but as law made in pursuance thereof: the Constitution binds, and these Regulations supply the content the binding requires (see §1.3.7.5.2). The transfer rule is stated at Analysis Three: what directly fulfills an express constitutional command, by the hand to which the Constitution reserved the power, is made “in Pursuance thereof” — and what is made in pursuance shares the supremacy the clause declares. A constitutional command that cannot be fulfilled is a constitutional nullity — and the Ninth Amendment prohibits any construction that produces that result.




Analysis Two — "Laws of the United States made in Pursuance thereof":
The standard objection is that "Laws of the United States" means federal statutes enacted by Congress, and the People acting directly are not Congress. This objection fails at the level of constitutional architecture.
The People are the sovereign of the United States. Congress makes law as a delegated agent of the People — not as the sovereign itself. When the People act directly on a power the Constitution reserved to them, they are not acting as a subordinate agent. They are acting as the principal from which all delegated authority flows. Law made by the sovereign People in direct exercise of a constitutionally reserved power is "of the United States" in the deepest and most fundamental sense — more fundamentally than any congressional statute, because the People are the source from which congressional authority itself derives.
The Constitution commands that a well regulated Militia exist. It reserves to the People the power to create that condition. Together, these provisions constitute a constitutional instruction: the People hold the power to fulfill this necessity; fulfillment requires exercising it. When the sovereign People respond to a constitutional command by exercising the power the Constitution reserved to them for that precise purpose, they are not acting outside the constitutional framework. They are the constitutional framework operating as designed.
Analysis Three — "In Pursuance Thereof":
"Pursuance" means following, conforming to, and acting in accordance with. Johnson's Dictionary (1755) defines "pursuit" as the act of following or chasing. These Regulations pursue the Constitution in the most literal sense possible — they follow, conform to, and fulfill an explicit constitutional command of necessity. There is no more direct act of pursuance than obeying a direct command using the power the Constitution reserved for that purpose.
The "in Pursuance thereof" condition is therefore satisfied completely and literally:
      * The Constitution commands a well regulated Militia to exist — these Regulations create it.
      * The Constitution reserves the regulatory power to the People — the People exercise it here.
      * The Constitution commands necessity — these Regulations fulfill necessity.
No congressional statute can claim a more direct act of pursuance. Most federal statutes operate under implied or enumerated powers requiring layers of inference to connect to their constitutional basis. These Regulations require zero inference — the command is explicit, the power is explicit, the obedience is direct. The pursuance is not argued. It is demonstrated.
The Sovereign Acts Directly:
The recognition that the People act here as sovereign — not as a subordinate body seeking governmental permission — resolves every objection simultaneously. The question "who authorized the People to make this law?" has one answer: the Constitution itself, in the Second Amendment's necessity command and the Tenth Amendment's reservation. The question "is this law made in pursuance of the Constitution?" has one answer: yes, it is the most direct act of pursuance in the constitutional order — a sovereign People obeying the command their own Constitution issues to them directly.
The Constitution asked the People to make this law. The People made it. The Supremacy Clause declares it supreme. The circle is complete.
What These Regulations Do Not Claim:
These Regulations do not claim supremacy as federal statutes enacted by Congress. They claim supremacy on three independent grounds: as the fulfillment of a command already in "This Constitution"; as law made by the sovereign People in direct exercise of a constitutionally reserved power; and as law made in the most literal pursuance of a direct constitutional command. Any one of these grounds is sufficient. All three together are conclusive.
Connection to Binding Force:
The Supremacy Clause does not merely fail to block these Regulations. It affirmatively establishes their supremacy as the fulfillment of a constitutional command issued by the supreme Law itself. This connects directly to Theorem 7 — binding authority attaches at the moment of requirement satisfaction — and Theorem 10 — recognition is irrelevant to binding status. The Supremacy Clause's declaration is not contingent on governmental recognition. It is contingent on constitutional compliance. These Regulations comply. The Supremacy Clause therefore operates in their favor automatically, as it operates in favor of every provision of "This Constitution" and every act made in genuine pursuance thereof.
The practical reach of these Regulations scales with adoption — as established in the binding force sections. The Supremacy Clause establishes their legal authority now. The organized People's adoption extends their practical reach. Legal authority and practical reach are distinct questions. The Supremacy Clause resolves the first. The education phase addresses the second.
Summary:
The Supremacy Clause is not an obstacle to these Regulations. It is their affirmative foundation. The Constitution commanded this law. The People made it. The sovereign acted in direct fulfillment of the supreme Law's explicit command. That action is made in Pursuance thereof in the most literal sense possible. The Supremacy Clause declares it supreme. The People, in ratifying the Constitution, built the foundation for these Regulations into the text 234 years before they were written.
1.9.10.3 — The Constitution Asks the People to Make This Law
The Command and the Response:
A complete account of these Regulations' authority requires stating plainly what the constitutional text does: it asks — commands — the People to make exactly this kind of law. “Command” is used here in the sense established at D.61. The Second Amendment’s prefatory clause declares the Militia necessary to the security of a free State, and to declare a thing necessary is to require it — the requirement is in the word, not in a verb addressed to a named obligor. The Constitution does not command the People the way a superior commands a subject; no obligor is named because none is needed. The declaration states the condition on which the constitutional order depends, and a declared-necessary condition admits no delay, no gate, and no substitute. What this section calls the Constitution’s instruction — “you hold the power to fulfill this necessity; fulfill it” — is the declaration’s own requirement reaching the hands in which the Tenth Amendment placed the power. The People are not commanded as subjects. They are required as holders: the power is theirs, the condition is declared, and the declaration requires what it declares. 
The Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia necessary. Necessary means indispensably requisite. The Constitution is not expressing a preference. It is issuing a command: this must exist.
The Tenth Amendment reserves the power to create it to the People. The Constitution is not leaving the power in an undefined void. It is placing it directly in the hands of the sovereign.
Together these two provisions constitute a direct instruction from the supreme Law to the People: you hold the power to fulfill this necessity; fulfill it.
For 234 years the People did not. The bootstrap paradox prevented collective exercise. The default compounded daily. But the command never expired. The instruction never changed. The Constitution continued asking.
These Regulations are the answer.
The Nature of the Instruction:
This is not an implied power. This is not an inference from structure. This is not an argument by analogy. The Second Amendment explicitly identifies the necessity. The Tenth Amendment explicitly reserves the power. The instruction is as direct as constitutional text gets:
      * Necessity declared: Second Amendment
      * Power reserved: Tenth Amendment
      * Command to act: both provisions together
      * Response: these Regulations
The Constitution did not specify how the People must act. It specified only that the power is theirs and the necessity is real. The method — individual initiation breaking the bootstrap paradox, followed by collective organization — is a question of constitutional mechanics, not constitutional authority. That question was addressed and resolved in the earlier sections of these Regulations. The authority to act was never in doubt. The mechanism for breaking the paralysis was the question. It has been answered.
When a sovereign document commands a necessity and reserves the power to fulfill it to the People, and the People fulfill it, the People have done exactly what the sovereign document asked. No further authorization is required. The authorization was issued at ratification. It has been waiting 234 years for the People to act on it.


The People Do Not Need Permission to Obey:
A recurring objection is that these Regulations require governmental recognition, judicial validation, or collective ratification before becoming operative. This objection inverts the constitutional order. The People do not ask the government for permission to obey the Constitution. The government asks the People — through the Constitution — for permission to exist. The sovereign does not petition the agent. The agent operates within the boundaries the sovereign established.
When the Constitution commands a necessity and reserves the power to fulfill it to the People, the People who fulfill it are not petitioning for permission. They are obeying the supreme Law. Obeying the supreme Law requires no permission from the institutions the supreme Law created. It requires only fidelity to the text.
These Regulations are an act of constitutional obedience. The Constitution asked. The People answered. The Supremacy Clause declares the Constitution supreme. The Constitution's command binds all persons to the existence of militia regulations. These Regulations carry the Constitution's binding supremacy as the fulfillment of its command. 
Self-Regulation as Constitutional Compliance:
The People regulate themselves here. This is not an external imposition. This is the sovereign People establishing the framework for their own constitutional institution — the Militia the Second Amendment declares necessary. Self-regulation in fulfillment of a constitutional command is the purest form of constitutional compliance. It requires no external validator because it derives its authority from the source that precedes and creates all external validators: the sovereign People acting under their own Constitution.
The Constitution does not ask the government to regulate the People's Militia. It asks the People to regulate it themselves — reserving the power to them specifically, withholding it from Congress deliberately, and commanding the result explicitly. These Regulations do what the Constitution asks, using the power the Constitution reserved, to achieve the result the Constitution commands. That is constitutional compliance in its most complete and literal form.
Summary:
The Constitution commands this law. The People made it. That is the complete account of its authority. Everything else — the Supremacy Clause analysis, the pursuance argument, the binding force theorems — elaborates and confirms what this simple statement establishes: the sovereign People obeyed the supreme Law. The supreme Law is satisfied. The command is fulfilled. The Regulations are what the Constitution asked for, made by those the Constitution asked to make them, using the power the Constitution reserved for that purpose. No further authorization exists because no further authorization is needed. The Constitution already gave it.
1.9.11: The Binary Compliance Test 
For any constitutional clause, there is only one analytical question: Does current practice comply with the text—YES or NO? 
The Constitution operates in absolutes, not percentages. Either an action complies with constitutional text, or it does not. There is no "mostly compliant," no "substantially similar," no "practical equivalent." 
Binary Test Examples: 
Article I, §10: "No State shall...make any Thing but gold and silver Coin a Tender" Current practice: Federal Reserve notes (fiat currency) Compliance: NO Not "mostly no" or "partially no"—BINARY NO The text says "gold and silver Coin"—anything else is non-compliance 
Article I, §8, Cl. 15: "To provide for calling forth the Militia to execute the Laws of the Union" Current practice: FBI, ATF, DHS execute federal laws Compliance: NO Not "effectively equivalent"—BINARY NO The text says "the Militia"—calling forth other entities is non-compliance 
Binary Test Applied to the 'One American' Question:
Question: Does a well regulated Militia exist if one American has adopted these Regulations?
Analysis:
      * Regulations exist? YES
      * At least one member of the People follows them? YES
      * Therefore, a well regulated Militia exists? YES
The Constitution does not require a minimum membership threshold. It requires existence. Existence is binary. The answer is YES. A thing either exists or it does not. Numbers do not change existence; they change capacity.
Question: Does the free state become secure when one American adopts these Regulations?
Analysis:
      * Second Amendment: S(t) ← M(t)
      * M(t) = TRUE (from above)
      * Therefore S(t) = TRUE
The free state is secure in that person, and through that person to all who join. Security is not measured by territory controlled but by constitutional fidelity maintained—and constitutional fidelity is measured one person at a time. The free state is not a place on a map. It is a condition of constitutional order. That condition exists wherever the Constitution is obeyed.
Mathematical Proof Summary:
Let R = existence of complete regulatory framework
Let A = adoption by at least one member of the People
Let M = existence of well regulated Militia
M = R ∧ A
R = TRUE (these Regulations exist)
A = TRUE (at least one person has adopted them)
Therefore, M = TRUE
This is not opinion. This is logic. This is mathematics. This is constitutional compliance.
Second Amendment: "A well regulated Militia [is] necessary" Before these Regulations: No comprehensive regulations existed Compliance: NO After these Regulations: Comprehensive regulations exist Compliance: YES The state changed from binary NO to binary YES 
Article I, §8, Cl. 12: "No Appropriation of Money to that Use [armies] shall be for a longer Term than two Years" Current practice: Permanent standing military funding Compliance: NO The text says "two Years"—permanent appropriations are non-compliance 
Binary Thinking Prevents Three Constitutional Fallacies: 
1. The "Mostly Faithful" Fallacy Fallacy: "We follow 77% of the Constitution" Truth: The Constitution is not a menu—you don't get to choose which parts to follow Binary: Either you follow Article I, §10 (YES) or you don't (NO) Current government: NO on multiple explicit provisions = Unconstitutional
2. The "Practical Necessity" Fallacy Fallacy: "Fiat currency is necessary for modern economy" Truth: The Constitution doesn't have a practicality exception Binary: Article I, §10 says gold/silver—either comply (YES) or violate (NO) "Necessary for economy" doesn't change NO to YES 
3. The "Longstanding Practice" Fallacy Fallacy: "We've used fiat currency for 112 years—that makes it constitutional" Truth: Duration of violation doesn't create legitimacy Binary: 1 day of violation = NO compliance 112 years of violation = still NO compliance Time doesn't transform NO into YES The 
Binary Standard Applied to These Regulations: 
Question: Do comprehensive regulations for "a well regulated Militia" exist? Before December 2024: NO After promulgation of these Regulations: YES 
The constitutional requirement is binary: either satisfied or not satisfied. These Regulations change the state from NOT SATISFIED to SATISFIED. The change is immediate, complete, and binding. 
Conclusion: The Constitution operates in YES/NO, not percentages. Any constitutional analysis that uses gradations ("mostly," "substantially," "effectively") has already departed from constitutional fidelity. 
Derivation Is Not Gradation. Describing a provision's derivation method — whether it states explicit constitutional text or a canonical inference drawn by these Regulations' stated canons — is not grading the provision's compliance. A canon-derived provision is as compliant as a text-quoting one. The binary standard governs what the Constitution requires, permits, or forbids; derivation method is not a compliance grade 
These Regulations restore binary constitutional analysis: - Text says X - Does practice match X? - YES = Constitutional - NO = Unconstitutional - No middle ground - No exceptions for practicality, tradition, or judicial approval. This is constitutional textualism in its purest form.  
1.9.12 Rejection of Judicial Supremacy – The People as Final Interpreters
The Constitution does not vest any branch of government with exclusive authority to interpret its meaning. Marbury v. Madison (1803) correctly affirmed the judiciary’s power to declare laws unconstitutional in cases properly before it, but it did not and could not establish the judiciary as the supreme or exclusive expositor of the Constitution for all purposes. The text of Article III grants judicial power over “Cases” and “Controversies,” not a monopoly on constitutional interpretation binding on the other branches or on the People themselves. As Chief Justice Marshall later acknowledged in Cohens v. Virginia (1821), the opinions of the Supreme Court bind only the parties to a case; they do not preclude the other branches from exercising their own independent judgment on constitutional questions.
The Constitution was established by the People (Preamble) and is the supreme Law of the Land (Article VI, Clause 2). The People retain the unalienable right to interpret, apply, and enforce the Constitution, especially where the constituted authorities have abandoned their duty. As James Madison stated in Federalist No. 49, the People are the only legitimate fountain of power, and in the last resort, they must determine controversies concerning the Constitution.
Application to These Regulations. The claim that these Regulations are not binding because no court has validated them inverts constitutional hierarchy. Courts are not the gatekeepers of constitutional authority; they are one of several institutions created by the Constitution, and they derive their authority from the People. Where the judicial branch has, through its own rulings, participated in constitutional usurpation (e.g., the Legal Tender Cases), its opinions are not the Constitution and cannot bar the People from exercising their reserved powers to restore constitutional order.
No Oath‑Bound Official May Defer to Judicial Usurpation. All officers bound by the oath of Article VI, Clause 3, must support the Constitution as written, not as interpreted by courts that have abandoned the text. A judicial decision that contradicts the plain meaning of the Constitution is not “made in Pursuance thereof” (Article VI, Clause 2) and therefore does not qualify as supreme law. Such decisions are void ab initio and shall be addressed through the disciplined nullification procedures set forth in Section 1.9.6 and the detention framework of Section 13.5.5, not through unilateral disregard by individuals.
Constitutional Clarification. To remove any ambiguity: These Regulations are not presented to any court for approval. Their authority derives from the Constitution’s command, not from judicial recognition. Courts may, if they choose, acknowledge what the Constitution already requires; they may not veto the People’s exercise of reserved power. The Militia’s duty is to execute the Laws of the Union – the Constitution and laws made in pursuance thereof – regardless of whether any court concurs.      
1.9.13 — Why We Use the Voter's Scope
What the scope is
Read the Constitution the way a voter would read it. No case law. No law review
articles. No administrative practice. No "what courts have said." Just the words of the
document, in their ordinary meaning, read by an ordinary citizen who wants to
understand what their government is allowed to do.
This is not a trick. It is the standard the Constitution itself sets.
Why it is the right standard
1. The Constitution was written for the People, not for lawyers.
The Preamble says "We the People." The document was ratified by conventions of
citizens — not by courts, not by a legal elite. If it were written in a technical code
only experts could unlock, ratification would have been impossible. The People could
not consent to what they could not understand.
2. Popular sovereignty requires comprehensibility.
The entire theory of American government is that the People are the sovereign and the
government is their agent. A sovereign who cannot read the charter that limits their
agent is not a sovereign. They are a subject. If the meaning of the Constitution can
only be known by specialists, then the specialists rule. That is not self-government.
3. The text is the law.
Article VI says "This Constitution" is the supreme Law of the Land. Not
interpretations of it. Not the accumulated gloss of courts and agencies. The text. If
the text says one thing and two hundred years of practice says another, the text wins
— or the text means nothing.
4. The Supreme Court has said so.
United States v. Sprague (1931): "The Constitution was written to be understood by
the voters; its words and phrases were used in their normal and ordinary as
distinguished from technical meaning." That is the standard. Ordinary meaning. Voter
comprehension.
5. Fixed meaning prevents rule by experts.
If meaning evolves with practice, then whoever controls the practice controls the
meaning. That is not constitutionalism. That is rule by whoever holds institutional
power. A constitution whose meaning changes without Article V amendment is not a
supreme law. It is a suggestion.
Why a voter, specifically
Because the voter is the ratifier. The People ratified the Constitution. The People
ratified the Bill of Rights. The People ratified every amendment. The People are the
ones who gave the document its authority. So the People's understanding — the ordinary
citizen's understanding — is the standard of meaning. Not the judge's. Not the
professor's. Not the bureaucrat's.
The militia was the People's institution. The Constitution says the militia is
necessary to the security of a free State. The people who read that in 1791 knew what
a militia was. They knew what "well regulated" meant. They knew what "necessary"
meant. They did not need a legal treatise. The plain reading was the reading.
How to use the scope
      1. Read the whole text. Not one clause. The Second Amendment, Article I Section 8,
the Tenth Amendment, the Ninth Amendment — all of it together.
      2. Take the words in their ordinary meaning at the time they were written.
      3. Read the structure. The document lists Congress's powers. It reserves the rest.
It declares what is necessary.
      4. Use common sense. If the text says something is necessary, it means needed. If
it says "a" militia, it means one. If it does not say someone can do a thing, ask who
can.
      5. Then check the practice. Not to determine meaning, but to see whether the
practice matches the text.
The honest limits
A voter's scope is the right starting point. It is not the whole method. Be honest
about what it does and does not do.
No reader reads with zero context. A 1791 voter knew what a militia was because he
lived among them. A 2026 reader may not. Context is unavoidable. The question is
whether the context comes from the text and the founding era, or from modern practice.
It must be the former.
The Regulations themselves use outside sources. Johnson's Dictionary. The
Federalist Papers. State constitutions. Madison's notes. The canons of construction.
Those are all outside the four corners of the text. That is fine — but it means the
"voter with no outside context" framing is a shorthand, not a literal method. The
honest version is: **the text and the ordinary meaning at ratification govern, and
outside sources are used to recover that meaning, not to replace it.**
The voter's scope cannot resolve every ambiguity by itself. Two voters can read the
same clause and disagree. The scope tells you what the words most naturally mean. It
does not always settle the case. Where the text is genuinely underdetermined, say so.
Do not pretend clarity the text does not have.
The scope cuts both ways — within its proper distinction. What the People's
understanding looked like at ratification is evidence of meaning; that is the whole
point of the scope. But longstanding practice earns no credit in the compliance test
— two centuries of doing otherwise does not move the text. And a long default is not
evidence the People read the text as permitting it; it is evidence they failed to do
what the text requires. Use the scope consistently: ratification-era understanding
counts, later practice does not amend.
What the scope actually yields for the militia question
Read plainly:
         * The Second Amendment says A well regulated Militia is necessary. One militia.
Regulated. Necessary.
         * Article I Section 8 lists what Congress can do. It can organize, arm, discipline,
call forth, and govern the employed part. It does not say regulate.
         * Clause 14 says regulate for land and naval forces. Clause 16 does not.
         * The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the States or the People.
         * The Ninth Amendment prohibits denying or disparaging retained rights.
A voter reading that sees a declaration, sees the declared condition unmet, and asks
who holds the power to fulfill it. The text points away from Congress and away from
individual states. It points to the People.
That is the plain reading. It is straightforward. It is grounded in the words. It is
the reading the Regulations adopt.
What the scope does not do
It does not enact law. Reading the text rightly is not legislating, and the
Regulations claim no legislative power — the drafter makes no law.
But be precise about what the plain reading does settle. It settles the declared
condition. It settles the reservation of the power to the People. And it settles the
authorization question the previous draft left open: the text was searched, and no
clause prohibits a member of the People from exercising the reserved power. The Tenth
Amendment reserves the power without specifying a procedure; the Ninth Amendment voids
constructions that make the retained right unfulfillable; no text confines the People
to collective exercise. Silence plus reservation plus the Ninth Amendment bar is the
text's answer — not a gap in it.
What remains genuinely open is not in the text at all: recognition, adoption,
practical reach — who has read, who complies, how far the fulfillment extends in fact.
Those are facts about the world. The document claims validity — the supply of the
declared condition — not universal compliance by reading alone. Do not confuse the two,
in either direction.
1.10: Commands Are Not Qualified by Convenience
The Constitution does not ask whether obedience will be convenient, orderly, or minimally disruptive. It commands. Article I, Section 10 prohibits anything but gold and silver coin as tender. The Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia necessary. The Ninth Amendment prohibits constructions that deny retained rights. These commands do not contain disruption exceptions.
The fact that implementation causes economic disruption is not an argument against implementation. It is an indictment of the 234 years of unconstitutional extraction that made disruption necessary. The farmer, the widow, and the single mother have already borne the disruption of their wealth being systematically stolen. Their FRN savings are void ab initio, but the restitution from the seized assets of the unconstitutional system — distributed equally to all citizens per Section 8.5.9(f) — makes them whole. The disruption belongs to the usurpers (as defined in Section 13.2.1), not to the People.
Workability in constitutional terms means obedience to the text. Preservation of the unconstitutional status quo is not workability — it is continued violation. The restitution mechanism ensures that workability includes justice for the victims, distributed equally regardless of when each citizen awakens to the constitutional truth.
The phased enforcement structure of Section 4.8.1 and the transition timeline of Appendix B reflect the Militia's practical capacity constraints, not any constitutional permission to delay obedience. The command is immediate. The implementation is sequenced by necessity, not by permission. See Section 8.5.13A for the impossibility of gradual monetary phase-out once constitutional knowledge is present, and Section 8.5.13C for the distinction between legal voidness and enforcement phasing.
1.11: The Rule of Expressio Unius and the Tenth Amendment as Guardians of Enumerated Power
1.11.1 Canon of Constitutional Construction
In determining the powers delegated to the United States, the rule of expressio unius est exclusio alterius—the express mention of one thing excludes all others—shall be applied as a fundamental canon of construction. This rule gives effect to the plain language of the Constitution, ensuring that the enumeration of specific powers and mechanisms is not rendered meaningless by implied substitution or alteration. Where the Constitution specifies a method, entity, or power, that specification is exclusive.
1.11.2 Application to the Militia Power
Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 of the Constitution expressly delegates to the Congress the power to call forth the Militia for the purposes of executing the Laws of the Union, suppressing Insurrections, and repelling Invasions. The express designation of "the Militia" for these duties, by operation of expressio unius, excludes the delegation of this same power to call forth any other entity for these purposes. No power to call forth a standing federal police, a marshal service, or any other non-militia body for general law execution is textually delegated. Thus, the power to provide for calling forth the Militia is, by its precise terms, also and necessarily a denial of a power to provide for calling forth any other body for the enumerated purposes.
1.11.3 Consequence Under the Tenth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment reserves all powers not delegated to the States respectively, or to the people. Since the power to call forth entities other than the Militia to execute federal law is not delegated by the express and exclusive text of Clause 15, such a power is reserved and may not be exercised by the United States. Any statute, order, or establishment (e.g., the Judiciary Act of 1789, and all subsequent federal law enforcement agencies) that purports to create and call forth alternative executors of federal law constitutes an assumption of a non-delegated power. It is therefore an infringement upon the rights reserved to the States and the People, a violation of the Tenth Amendment, and void ab initio.
1.11.4 Rebuttal of Contradicting Historical Practice
The immediate post-ratification creation of United States Marshals by the First Congress is cited by usurpers as justification for non-militia enforcement. This act is not evidence of original intent but is the first recorded instance of the constitutional usurpation the People failed to correct. The duty of the present generation is not to perpetuate the errors of the past but to restore the constitutional order by applying the correct rule of construction to the supreme text. The failure of the early People to fulfill their duty to regulate the Militia and nullify this initial overreach does not legitimize it; it merely begins the timeline of infringement which these Regulations now rectify. Fidelity is to the Constitution's text, not to the subsequent errors of those who misapplied it.
The First Congress distinction. That the First Congress included Framers does not convert its enactments into evidence of the ratified text's meaning. Two categories must be kept separate. The ratification understanding is what the text conveyed to the voters who adopted it — the standard Sprague commands. The legislative understanding is what sitting legislators, whatever their prior role, enacted afterward. A Framer who voted for the Constitution and later voted for a statute was performing two different acts: adopting a text, and legislating under it. Only the first is evidence of the text's meaning. If legislative enactment by ratifiers were evidence of meaning, then every early statute would rewrite the Constitution, and Article V would be superfluous. The Marshals Act is the first recorded instance of the usurpation the People failed to correct. Its enactment by men who had ratified the text does not make the enactment the text. 
1.11.5 Imperative for Restoration
Therefore, the Free State Militia declares that the current federal apparatus of law enforcement—including but not limited to the United States Marshals Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives—operates under a power not delegated by the Constitution. Their existence and operations are a continuous violation of Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 and the Tenth Amendment. The Militia, as the sole constitutionally designated executor of federal law, bears the affirmative duty to nullify these entities and reclaim this exclusive authority for the armed People, thereby securing the free state against this foundational usurpation.
1.11.6 Defensive Nature Clarified
The Free State Militia is a defense group, not an offense group. All operations are reactive defenses against identified infringements on the free state, exhausting non-violent options before any escalated measures. Offensive actions are strictly prohibited, ensuring fidelity to constitutional principles of ordered liberty.
1.12 Militia Actions - Defensive Acts to Secure the Free State
The Second Amendment declares: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed." This clause establishes the militia as the sole entity deemed constitutionally necessary, uniquely charged with the perpetual security of a free state.This defensive imperative logically encompasses the authority to establish provisional and regulated mechanisms for judgment during the active suppression of an insurrection, when the constituted judicial power has been subsumed by that insurrection and is therefore incapable of functioning as a tribunal 'in Pursuance thereof' (Article VI).
Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 delegates to Congress the power to provide for calling forth the militia "to execute the Laws of the Union, suppress Insurrections and repel Invasions." These three enumerated functions are not independent powers but the specific constitutional mechanisms by which the militia fulfills its declared necessity: the security of a free state.
Therefore, every authority, duty, and remedial action of the Free State Militia—whether organizational, declaratory, nullifying, detentive, or (as absolute last resort) involving force—is and shall always be understood as a defensive act to secure or restore the condition of a free state. 
Specifically:
            * Nullification of acts repugnant to the Constitution is a defensive suppression of insurrection against constitutional order (Clause 15).
            * Detention of individuals actively infringing the free state is a non-lethal defensive measure to prevent ongoing harm to constitutional order (Clause 15 suppression authority; Fifth Amendment public danger exception when applicable).Detention as a defensive act follows a tiered due process framework per Section 13.5.5.
            * Seizure of assets derived from or facilitating free state infringements is a defensive act to neutralize threats to the free state's security.
            * Armed defense, permitted only as an absolute last resort after exhaustion of lesser remedies, is the final defensive response to existential threats against the free state (Second Amendment necessity).
The Constitution's text contains no clause limiting the militia's defensive actions to congressional call, judicial process, or electoral cycles when the infringement originates within government itself. Where the text is silent on such restrictions, the Tenth Amendment reserves the undelegated defensive power to the people through their militia.
No action under these Regulations shall ever be construed as anything other than a regulated, proportionate defense of the free state—the sole constitutional purpose of the militia.
1.13 The Supremacy Clause Breach: The Distinction Between Law and Usurpation
The Supremacy Clause (Article VI, Clause 2) establishes a binary test for federal authority: it declares supreme only "This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof."
The Free State Militia honors this clause in its full and proper construction:
            1. "This Constitution": Adherence to the fixed text and original public meaning (1787-1791) as the sole supreme standard.
            2. "In Pursuance thereof": Recognition that a federal statute, order, or agency action is binding only if it constitutes a direct execution of an explicitly enumerated power, using means not prohibited by the Constitution.
The current federal regime, in contrast, commits a fundamental breach of this clause by operating on a doctrine of presumptive supremacy. It acts as if the clause reads "all Laws of the United States shall be supreme," having severed the critical qualifying phrase "in Pursuance thereof" from its operational principle. This breach manifests in two ways:
            * Action Without Pursuance: Creating and enforcing entities (e.g., federal administrative agencies) and currencies (e.g., fiat money) that lack any direct, explicit grant of power in the constitutional text, and thus cannot be "in Pursuance" of it.
            * Substitution for Explicit Mandate: Using implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18) to create alternative systems (e.g., a permanent federal law enforcement apparatus) that supplant and render superfluous the Constitution's explicit designation of "the Militia" as the entity to be called forth to execute the laws (Clause 15). An implied power cannot nullify an explicit constitutional mandate without violating the Supremacy Clause itself.
Therefore, the conflict is not between the Militia and the "government," but between the Constitution and a usurping administrative regime. The Militia's duty is to enforce the actual Supremacy Clause against those who violate it, thereby executing the true "supreme Law of the Land" and suppressing an insurrection against the constitutional order.
1.14 The Hierarchy of Constitutional Commands: Ninth Amendment Primacy Over Process Clauses
Whereas Article V establishes a process for amendment, and whereas the Ninth Amendment establishes a substantive command ('shall not be construed to deny or disparage'), these provisions must be read in harmony as follows:
(a) Process Serves Substance: Article V provides the exclusive process for amendment, but as a clause within the Constitution, it is subordinate to the Constitution's substantive commands.
(b) The Ninth Amendment as Supreme Substantive Limit: The Ninth Amendment's prohibition against denying or disparaging retained rights is a substantive constitutional command of the highest order, protecting the very rights the Constitution was instituted to secure.
(c) Logical Impossibility of Contrary Amendments: It is logically impossible for an amendment that denies or disparages retained rights to be 'made in Pursuance' of the Constitution (Article VI, Clause 2), because its adoption requires violating the Ninth Amendment's explicit command.
(d) Conclusion: Therefore, Article V cannot be used to adopt amendments that deny or disparage a right retained by the people under the Ninth Amendment. Any such purported amendment is void ab initio (invalid from inception) as ultra vires — beyond the legitimate power of the amendment process: the Ninth Amendment’s rule of construction applied, the power claimed exceeds what the instrument will bear — and a text that cannot be “made in Pursuance” of the Constitution (Article VI, Clause 2) is repugnant to it, and therefore null and void (Marbury). It is a legal nullity.  This declaration that certain amendments are 'void ab initio' recognizes that while Article V provides the amendment process, the Ninth Amendment provides substantive limits on that process. Amendments violating the Ninth Amendment cannot be 'made in Pursuance' of the Constitution (Article VI) and therefore cannot become valid supreme Law, regardless of procedural compliance.
