Against this consistent usage, Clause 16 grants only "organizing, arming, and disciplining" — three narrower verbs, each distinctly defined in Johnson's Dictionary (1755) (organize: “To construct so as that one part co-operates with another; to form organically” (Johnson’s Dictionary, 1755); arm: "to furnish with weapons of offence"; discipline: Johnson’s Dictionary (1755), verb sense 1 “To educate; to instruct; to bring up” and verb sense 2 “To regulate; to keep in order” (the Regulations’ wording compounds the two genuine senses).” Under the canon of meaningful variation, the variation in the enacted text carries meaning; the canon operates on the text as adopted and requires no documentation of the drafters' deliberation. Supporting data point: the Articles of Confederation's "well-regulated and disciplined militia" treats "regulated" and "disciplined" as distinct qualities — the founding generation did not use the terms interchangeably. This strengthens the expressio unius inference with intratextual and lexical evidence. Presented as support for the inference, marked as such — not as standalone proof, and not as a claim about the Convention's deliberation. 
D.43 THE MASON-NEGLECT OBJECTION — ANSWERED. 
George Mason on congressional neglect, Virginia Ratifying Convention, June 14, 1788 (Elliot 3:380): "The general government ought, at the same time, to have some such power. But we need not give them power to abolish our militia. If they neglect to arm them, and prescribe proper discipline, they will be of no use." Mason — who had thrice proposed "to regulate" on August 18, 1787 — assumed Congress possessed the arming and disciplining power and feared its neglect, not its absence. Virginia's proposed amendments (June 27, 1788), item 11, supplied the remedy: "That each state respectively shall have the power to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining its own militia, whensoever Congress shall omit or neglect to provide for the same." Honest assessment: Mason's diagnosis — congressional omission/neglect of the militia power as a constitutional danger — is confirmed on the founding-era record, and it aligns with the account of congressional non-performance of the enumerated powers. His proposed remedy was state fallback, not direct popular action — a federalism data point consistent with the concession in S3 that the states hold a textual role. The document's Tenth Amendment remedy (the People's reserved power) is a separate inference, marked as such; Mason neither made nor foreclosed it. (Verification note: the June 14, 1788 quotation and Virginia item 11 text were not independently re-verified. See Part IX.) 
D.44 THE PENNSYLVANIA DISSENT — SUPPORT. 
Dissent of the Minority, Pennsylvania Convention, December 12, 1787, item 11: "That the power of organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia (the manner of disciplining the militia to be prescribed by Congress) remain with the individual states." The Constitution's fiercest contemporary critics read Clause 16 as granting Congress exactly these three powers — no more, no less — and sought to move them to the states by amendment. This confirms the ratification-era understanding that the grant consisted of the three enumerated verbs, consistent with the document's "three enumerated powers" reading (Appendix C.20). It does not address the broader "regulate" power either way; the Dissenters' quarrel was with federal monopoly of the three powers, not with the withholding inference. 
D.45 THE STATE-CONSTITUTIONS SURVEY — SUPPORT WITH COUNTEREXAMPLE RECORDED. 
The founding-era constitutional instruments of all thirteen original states surveyed (DE, GA, MA, NC, NH, NJ, NY, PA, SC, VA constitutions and declarations; Maryland 1776, Constitution — November 11, 1776; Connecticut, Charter of 1662, April 23, 1662, in force as the state's constitution until 1818; Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, Charter of July 1663, in force as the state's constitution until 1843; Avalon Project texts from Thorpe's Federal and State Constitutions). Vermont's 1777 constitution was also surveyed and is recorded separately below — Vermont was not one of the thirteen original states (admitted 1791) and is not counted in the thirteen-state figure. Of the thirteen original states, exactly one granted "regulations" power over the militia: Pennsylvania 1776, Frame of Government, §5 — "The freemen of this commonwealth and their sons shall be trained and armed for its defence under such regulations, restrictions, and exceptions as the general assembly shall by law direct, preserving always to the people the right of choosing their colonels and all commissioned officers under that rank." Every other original state avoided the grant. The three instruments completing the set confirm the pattern: Maryland (1776) uses "well regulated militia" only descriptively (Declaration of Rights, Art. XXV — "That a well-regulated militia is the proper and natural defence of a free government"), reserves the sole "regulating" power — "the sole and exclusive right of regulating the internal government and police thereof" — to the people (Art. II), and grants the Governor only command authority over the militia: to "embody the militia" with Council consent and, when embodied, to "alone have the direction thereof" (Constitution, Art. XXXIII), plus appointment, suspension, and removal of militia officers (Art. XLVIII). Connecticut's 1662 charter grants only the power "to Assemble, Martial-Array, and put in warlike Posture the Inhabitants of the said Colony," and to commission persons "to lead and conduct the said Inhabitants" — command authority, with martial law, not a regulate grant. Rhode Island's 1663 charter grants only the power to nominate commanders and military officers "for the leading, conductinge and travneing vpp the inhabitants... in martiall afiaires," with authority to "assemble, exercise in arms, martiall array, and putt in warlyke posture" them — its one use of "regulate" is "to regulate and order the wave and manner of all elections to offices and places of trust," concerning elections, not the militia. The remaining constitutions and declarations stand as previously recorded: New York (1777, Art. XL) used "armed and disciplined"; Massachusetts (1780, ch. II, §1, art. VII) gave the governor power "to train, instruct, exercise and govern the militia"; the rest used "well regulated" only descriptively in rights-declarations or granted no militia power at all. Vermont (1777), surveyed as a separately labeled fourteenth data point, also avoided the grant. Honest assessment: (1) the PA grant covered "regulations, restrictions, and exceptions" for training and arming — the administrative level, arguably within the organize/arm/discipline family rather than the broad Clause-14 "regulate"; (2) it was paired with an express reservation to the people (officer elections); (3) it did not survive — Pennsylvania's 1790 constitution replaced it with "The freemen of this commonwealth shall be armed and disciplined for its defence... The militia officers shall be appointed, in such manner, and for such time as shall be directed by law," dropping the "regulations" grant entirely, before the federal Bill of Rights; (4) as a federal Tenth Amendment matter, state-internal allocations do not alter the federal enumeration; (5) statutory titles are not constitutional grants — Connecticut's pre-revolutionary militia statutes were titled "An Act for Regulating the Militia" (e.g., the 1712 act, secondary-reported), but a statute's title is not a constitutional power grant, and the charter in force as Connecticut's constitution granted no regulate power. Within the thirteen original states, twelve of thirteen avoided granting "regulate" as a militia-power grant; the pattern supports the inference as far as the survey reaches, and the single partial counterexample is recorded here with its limits stated. 
D.46 THE REGULATION-WITHOUT-GOVERNMENT OBJECTION — ANSWERED.
 "Well regulated presupposes a regulator with authority; in 1791 that meant government. A private draft cannot regulate." Answered: the objection confuses the agent of regulation with government as such. Johnson's "regulate" is "to adjust by rule or method; to direct" (D.42) — regulation by rule, not necessarily by coercive command. The withholding thesis locates the regulatory power in the People under the Tenth Amendment; these Regulations are the People's exercise of it: rules adjusting the militia's order, discipline, and readiness, promulgated by the People for themselves. The People are a constitutional agent — the Constitution's own initiator (Federalist 40) and the Tenth Amendment's residual holder. The document is the demonstration: regulation without government is regulation by rule rather than by command. Honest note: founding-era well-regulated militias were typically government-disciplined; the Regulations concern where the constitutional power resides, not what historical practice looked like. 
D.47 THE CONCURRENT-POWER QUESTION — ANSWERED. 
Is the People's regulatory power concurrent with Congress's enumerated functions, or triggered only by congressional default? Concurrent. Retained powers are not contingent — the Tenth Amendment reserves what was never delegated, without a trigger condition. Congressional performance of its enumerated organizing, arming, and disciplining functions does not extinguish the People's regulatory power, because that power was never Congress's to preempt. Mason's state-fallback remedy (D.43) addressed the enumerated powers' neglect; the People's regulatory power needs no neglect to exist. The boundary: the People's regulation cannot contradict Congress's faithful exercise of its enumerated verbs — what is made in Pursuance governs — but those verbs are bounded to their terms (D.42), and beyond them the field is the People's. 
Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 grants Congress power ‘To provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining, the Militia.’ Granted — not denied, not evaded. The question is what a granted power, exercised, does to a retained power unexercised. The answer is nothing. 
Preemption runs against competing grants, not against reservations the grant never touched. The Tenth Amendment reserves what was never delegated, without a trigger condition and without a sunset clause. The regulatory power over the Militia was never ceded to Congress or to the States; it is retained by the People. Congress’s exercise of its Clause 16 functions — the Militia Act of 1792, the Dick Act, Title 32 — governs the select and organized forces those statutes created. It does not preempt the People’s retained regulatory power over the whole body, because that power was never Congress’s to preempt. A delegated power exercised within its terms displaces nothing that was never delegated. 
The continuous exercise since 1792 proves the distinction rather than defeating it. What Clause 16’s exercise produced, at every step, is a select force: the 1792 Act’s enrolled subset, the Dick Act’s National Guard, Title 32’s organized militia. The constitutional command addresses the whole body — ‘A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State.’ The gap between the select force Congress built and the whole-body discipline the command requires is the default, measured in the text’s own terms: the whole body was never organized, never armed, never disciplined as the command requires. Two hundred thirty-four years of select-force legislation is two hundred thirty-four years of the whole-body command unfulfilled — and the 1792 Act proves the breach began at the beginning, Congress in violation of its own arming duty from the first statute (see §1.4.1 for the full textual analysis). 
The People’s regulatory power is concurrent, not contingent. It needs no default to exist — retained powers are not triggered, they are held. But the default determines the necessity of its exercise now: ‘necessary’ does not wait for the delegated branches to complete what they have not completed in two centuries. Individual initiation cures institutional default. These Regulations supply, under the reserved power itself, the content the command requires and the statutes never supplied. 
D.48 THE NOVELTY OBJECTION — ANSWERED.
 "No founder proposed the People's retained regulatory power as the answer to congressional neglect." True, and immaterial under Rule 6: the standard is the plain text, not the headcount of historical proponents. Federalist 40 authorizes informal, unauthorized initiation precisely because the People cannot move in concert without it — novelty of proposal is the expected condition, not a defect. The document marks the Tenth Amendment remedy as inference where it is inference (D.43's honest note); what is not marked as inference is the text itself: the withholding, the reservation, the command. A reading can be unprecedented and still be what the text says. 
D.49 THE MEMBERSHIP OBJECTION — ANSWERED.
"The 1792 Act defined the militia as free able bodied white males eighteen to forty-five. On what authority is the militia 'the body of the people'?" The Constitution's word is "the people": the Amendment secures "the right of the people," and the militia the clause describes is "composed of the body of the people." Heller reads "the people" as all members of the political community. The 1792 classification was Congress's statutory choice under its organizing power — an exercise of an enumerated function, not a constitutional definition of the body. Congress may organize the militia; it may not redefine the constitutional subject. "The body of the People capable of bearing arms" is the functional boundary the text implies — capability, not Congress's categories. Congress's categories may organize the body; they may not shrink it. 
D.50 THE COMPULSION QUESTION — ANSWERED. 
"Militia duty was historically compulsory — musters, fines. Does the retained power include compulsion, and does de-mandating gut the militia?" Two distinct questions. Whether the People's retained regulatory power includes the authority to compel service is a question for the People's collective governance through Section 11 — not for this initiating draft to decide. What this draft does is decline to build coercive machinery: de-mandating removes the document's imposition of coercion, not the Constitution's command, which binds in conscience and law regardless of the machinery built around it. The duty stands; the enforcement design is the People's to supply. A militia bound by duty but not yet equipped with enforcement is unexecuted, not gutted. 
D.51 THE "TROOPS" OBJECTION (ARTICLE I, §10) — ANSWERED. 
"No State shall, without the Consent of Congress, keep Troops in time of Peace — isn't the People's militia 'troops'?" The Constitution distinguishes them throughout: Clause 14 governs "the land and naval Forces"; Clause 16 governs "the Militia." Founding-era military usage did the same — Steuben's Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States (1779) treated the troops' discipline as distinct from the militia's. "Troops" in §10 means standing forces kept up — the thing the Declaration's grievances named and the state constitutions set against the militia (Virginia 1776 — Declaration of Rights §13: “a well regulated militia, composed of the body of the people, trained to arms, is the proper, natural, and safe defence of a free State” — the 1776 American use of “free State” in the nondespotic-country sense, and the militia as the body of the people; Pennsylvania 1776, Massachusetts 1780: the militia “the proper, natural, and safe defence”; standing armies “dangerous to liberty”). The People's militia is the constitutional alternative to troops, not an instance of them. 
D.52 THE STATES' BOUNDARY — STATED. 
If the states do not hold the general regulatory power, what exactly may they do? Exactly what the text assigns: the appointment of officers and the training of the Militia "according to the discipline prescribed by Congress" (Clause 16) — the S3 division — plus whatever their own constitutions assign within the federal bounds. What they may not do: disarm the militia (the right is the People's, and the Amendment forbids its infringement); refuse the textual role in a manner that defeats the declared-necessary end; or forbid the People's own regulatory exercise — no state can prohibit what the federal Constitution's reservation protects. The object is singular and national; the administration is shared exactly as the text provides; the regulatory power over the whole was never the states' to claim. 




D.53 THE INSTANCE QUESTION — ANSWERED. 
"Is this draft the exclusive faithful execution of the retained power, or one instance of it — and what makes it authoritative if the People may rewrite it?" An instance: the initiating one. Its authority is Federalist 40's — an informal, unauthorized proposition, essential because the People cannot move in concert without one, offered on its merits (S4). It binds as obedience to the constitutional command, not as the only possible regulations. The People retain full authority to examine, amend, and rebuild every part of this framework. Exclusivity would claim what initiation cannot; the Regulations are the obedience, not monopoly. 
D.54 THE DEAD-HAND OBJECTION — ANSWERED. 
"The Framers could not foresee autonomous weapons, cyber operations, unmanned systems — why does 1791 bind 2026?" The Amendment declares an end — "a well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State" — not a technology. Ends bind across technological change; means adapt. The Regulations' "soldier" — any entity, human, machine, or program, deployed by a government to perform a soldier's functions — is the adaptation the end requires: the principle — the body of the people, armed, disciplined, ready — scales, while the text freezes no musket. "Necessary" is present tense (H1/H2); the free State exists now; the command binds now. What the Framers could not foresee is irrelevant to whether the declared end is met — and it is not met.
 D.55 THE "PEOPLE = STATES" OBJECTION — ANSWERED.
 "In the Tenth Amendment, 'the people' means the people of the several states in their capacity — i.e., the states. The reservation therefore runs to the states, and there is no popular reserved power distinct from state power." The disjunctions answer is (1) The redundancy canon. "The States respectively, or to the people" would be redundant if both terms named the same holder — the disjunction's second term must add what the first does not. (2) The Bill of Rights consistency test (D.4). "The people" appears identically in the First ("right of the people peaceably to assemble"), Second ("right of the people to keep and bear arms"), Fourth ("right of the people to be secure"), and Ninth ("rights... retained by the people") — ratified together, by the same People. Reading the Tenth's "the people" as "the state governments" requires reading the Second's as a right of state governments and the Ninth's retained rights as retained by state governments — readings no one defends. (3) The Preamble. The Preamble identifies "We the People of the United States" as the Constitution's ordaining authority; that textual usage distinguishes the People from the States as governments. The better textual reading therefore treats the disjunction as naming two distinct holders, and the People's share is held as the co-tenancy §1.3.11 describes. 
D.56 THE "CARVE-OUT" OBJECTION — ANSWERED. 
"The Fifth Amendment exception is only a carve-out from grand-jury presentment procedure; it confers no holding authority." The technical reading is known and is not adopted. The ordinary reader of 1791 reads the exception as stating the cases in which persons may be held without presentment or indictment — cases arising in the land or naval forces, or in the Militia when in actual service in time of war or public danger. That is a statement about who may hold persons, not a procedural footnote. The ordinary reader takes "except" as governing the whole of what precedes it: "No person shall be held to answer for a capital, or otherwise infamous crime, unless on a presentment or indictment of a Grand Jury, except in cases arising in the land or naval forces, or in the Militia, when in actual service in time of War or public danger" — the exception modifies the holding itself, not merely the procedural form the holding takes. Under Sprague, the ordinary voter's reading of constitutional text controls over technical refinement: the refined reading is commentary, not text. The exception therefore stands as written in §5.4. 
D.57 THE PEACETIME STANDING-ARMY OBJECTION — ANSWERED. 
The objection: “To raise and support Armies” grants the power outright (Article I, Section 8, Clause 12). The Third Amendment presupposes soldiers in peacetime — “No Soldier shall, in time of peace be quartered in any house, without the consent of the Owner” — there would be nothing to quarter otherwise. Hamilton defended the grant at length (Federalist 24–26). The Anti-Federalists demanded a peacetime ban and were refused. Therefore the peacetime standing army is constitutional, and the Militia’s duties to resist it are void. Answered. The grant was never unconditioned. What the ratifiers refused as a ban they adopted as a control, in the same sentence: “but no Appropriation of Money to that Use shall be for a longer Term than two Years.” The refusal of the ban is an adopted fact. The adoption of the control in its place is an adopted fact. The control has a purpose, and the purpose is written into its mechanism: every two years, the representatives of the People must reauthorize — must ask, and answer, whether the Army remains necessary. The two-year limit is not a funding technicality. It is the recurring consent of the governed, applied to the instrument of force. The Constitution names peacetime as the default legal state. “In time of peace” (Third Amendment). “No State shall, without the Consent of Congress... keep Troops... in time of Peace” (Article I, Section 10) — the states are barred from the very thing in peacetime. War is the named exception: “time of War or public danger” (Fifth Amendment), and war is a discrete act — Congress declares it. The designated peacetime defense is the Militia: “the proper, natural, and safe defence” (Virginia 1776; Pennsylvania 1776; Massachusetts 1780), Madison’s bulwark against federal overreach (Federalist 46). The Third Amendment grants no power to raise armies; it regulates quartering. Its peace/war distinction confirms the structure: peace is the norm, stated first and without qualification — peacetime quartering is barred even by statute, requiring the Owner’s own consent — while war is the exception, governed “in a manner to be prescribed by law.” A peacetime army maintained continuously since the Korean War — never demobilized to a peacetime footing, never below two million active-duty personnel through the Cold War (CRS), in peace as in war, reauthorized year after year without the existence question ever being put — is the precise condition the control was adopted to prevent from becoming permanent. The generation that adopted the Constitution had named the peacetime standing army as a cause for dissolving allegiance: “He has kept among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislatures.” They did not prohibit armies. They prohibited armies beyond the reach of the People’s recurring consent. The Militia’s duty to resist the maintenance of such an army — including through non-appropriated means — stands. 
The generation’s warning, in its own words. Cato’s Letters — Trenchard and Gordon, read throughout America in the eighteenth century — gave the standing-army objection its classical form: “As armies long kept up, and grown part of the government, will soon engross the whole government, and can never be disbanded; so liberty long lost, can never be recovered. Is not this an awful lesson to free states, to be vigilant against a dreadful condition, which has no remedy?” The same writers stated the positive mark of the free state: “In free states, every man being a soldier, or quickly made so.” The Framing generation thus named the two poles these Regulations enforce: the free state is the armed citizenry formed as militia; its death is the standing army grown into the government. (Quoted via Volokh, supra; cross-verified in two independent secondary sources with identical wording)
D.58 THE NULLITY-AND-ENTOMBMENT OBJECTION — ANSWERED. 
The objection, in its final and ablest form, grants the premises and refuses the conclusion: the omission of “regulate” is real; undelegated powers are reserved; no national discipline has ever been prescribed; “the power sits unexercised” — and yet no member of the People may initiate the necessary regulations. Non-performance is “a practical shortfall”; the remedies are “ordinary.” Necessary — but never. We do not accept no to necessary. 
I. The admissions, now complete. The objector grants, on the record: “‘The federal government lacks authority’ is not itself the exercise of a reserved power.” “The power sits unexercised in the sense that no comprehensive national regulatory code has been produced by the text’s own mechanisms.” “Congress has never prescribed a single national discipline under Clause 16... The unifying element has not operated.” “Fifty separate state practices are not ‘the discipline.’ The unifying purpose of the grant has not been realized.” “Whether one labels that situation a placeholder (as a practical matter) or a long-running practical barrier, the legal conclusion is the same.” “The Constitution itself declares the necessity. No institutional actor is given a monopoly on recognizing whether the declared condition exists.” “The reservation to the People is not contingent on Congress first prescribing the discipline.” / “The People retain whatever residual authority the text actually leaves them.” On the sergeant: “Yes” — and “The Constitution is a lawful superior.” The gate is gone. Not “exercisable when Congress acts” — the objector denied the contingency. The People hold the power now: ungated, unmonopolized in recognition, declared by the Constitution itself — unexercised, and on the objection’s reading, unexercisable. A retained authority that may not be exercised is retained in name. The nullity no longer wears the Tenth Amendment’s words. It stands bare. The objector further affirms that the people’s rights — including the right to keep and bear arms — “remain intact,” and that “[n]othing in the answers given alters, suspends, or conditions those rights.” The dispute is narrowed to the status question. Rights were never at issue; the objector concedes it. 
II. The inventory is empty. The objector’s inventory of how a national-scope reserved power may be exercised: “through state governments” (impossible singly — admitted); “through individual rights” (a different category — conceded); “or simply by the federal government’s lack of authority” (conceded not to be exercise). Three entries; zero exercises. When the inventory of a constitutional provision’s exercise is empty, the provision is not being interpreted. It is being entombed. “Or to the people” names a holder. A holder holds something exercisable, or the Constitution deals in courtesies. It does not. 
III. “Available in principle” is the conceded placeholder. The text’s track, the objector now says, remains “available in principle even while historically unused.” Available to whom? To an actor that has not acted in 234 years, with no trigger ever — the objector’s own words. D.3’s description is conceded “fair,” and the label is now accepted either way: “placeholder (as a practical matter) or a long-running practical barrier.” A principle no one can invoke is not availability. It is D.3: “A mechanism that exists on paper but produces no result for 234 years is not a mechanism. It is a placeholder. The Constitution does not command placeholders; it commands results.” “Non-use is simply non-use” — for optional powers. This power’s exercise is declared necessary: indispensably requisite, the objector’s grant. Non-use of the necessary is not “simply non-use.” It is the necessity unmet — which is what makes 234 years constitutionally significant rather than historically unfortunate. The state-level escape is closed by the objector’s own hand. State training authority reads “according to the discipline prescribed by Congress” — conditioned on a discipline that does not exist. And: “Fifty separate state practices are not ‘the discipline.’” The grant says “the discipline” — singular, definite article. Unity is the grant’s entire purpose; the objector admits it “has not been realized.” The clock still needs its maker; fifty apprentices with no pattern are not regulation in the constitutional sense. 
IV. The false dilemma — and the lawful superior. “If the writing creates no new obligation and remains merely private exposition or advocacy, then it does not fulfill the necessity command as binding law. If it is claimed to fulfill the command as the operative framework, then it is being advanced as something more than private exposition.” The dilemma omits the third category: operative compliance with a pre-existing command. The obligation is the Constitution’s — pre-existing, granted (“necessary,” now), declared by the Constitution itself (the objector’s admission). The Regulations supply the content of compliance. The objector concedes the sergeant: “Yes.” A sergeant drilling troops to the prescribed discipline produces operative rules and legislates nothing; his orders bind no one beyond the lawful command, yet they are not “mere exposition.” That is what Q23 — granted throughout — describes: no new obligation, because the obligation is the command’s. The dilemma counts only legislation and literature, and omits obedience. The objector’s rule for obedience: the Constitution’s “commands are obeyed by acting within the powers and procedures it actually allocates.” The Tenth Amendment is a power the Constitution actually allocates — “reserved... to the people.” Acting under it is acting within the allocation, by the objector’s own rule. And “the Constitution is a lawful superior” — the objector’s words. A commander who orders the hill taken without specifying tactics authorizes tactical discretion; the mission is established, the means reserved. The “inside vs. establishing” distinction collapses: the Constitution established the necessity, the People supply the drill. The “Yes” stands; the distinction does not. No new capacity is created. Initiation under necessity, force from the command, correction retained by the holder (Section 11). That is a reserved power exercised by the one to whom the text reserved it — the mode of power-exercising the text establishes, not a mode of law making it never did.
 V. The trilemma, unanswered. Indispensably requisite (granted). Never satisfied in 234 years (granted). Secure free States existing throughout (the objector’s presupposition). The objector’s only exit was state-level satisfaction of “well regulated” — and the objector then admitted: “Fifty separate state practices are not ‘the discipline.’ The unifying purpose of the grant has not been realized.” The exit is closed by the one who opened it. What remains: a necessity never met, a reservation never exercised, a holder forbidden to hold — ungated, unmonopolized, declared by the text itself. The nullity and the entombment, confessed in the objector’s own words. We do not accept no to necessary. The command is present-tense. The power is reserved to the People. The People have acted. The Regulations are the exercise: the Militia is regulated, the free state is defined, the necessity is met — now, as the text commands. 
D.59 THE INTERLOCUTOR CONDEMNS ITS OWN CONSTRUCTION  
The interlocutor was asked, under strict 1787–1791 text and ordinary meaning, whether the Regulations are binding supreme law. It answered no. The exchange then proceeded through eight rounds of textual examination. What follows is not a characterization of the interlocutor's position. It records the interlocutor's position in the interlocutor's own words, assembled. 
 I. The Ninth Amendment tripwire — granted. Asked whether a construction that renders a retained right inescapably unexercisable by its own terms denies or disparages that right within the meaning of the Ninth Amendment, the interlocutor answered: “Yes: a construction that renders a retained right inescapably unexercisable by its own terms denies or disparages that right within the meaning of the Ninth Amendment.” The interlocutor disputes that the right to the well regulated Militia is retained. The conditional is granted. And the interlocutor’s own construction is the trigger. The interlocutor holds, in its own words: • The sole permitted method: “The constitutional method for producing and activating the Militia is the method those clauses establish.” (Article I, §8, Clauses 15–16.) • The admitted record: “Congress has at various times prescribed organizing, arming, and disciplining frameworks under Clause 16. No single, permanent, comprehensive national regulatory code... has been prescribed.” “None of these supplies a complete, permanent, whole-body discipline of the kind the document demands.” • The prohibited alternative: “none by itself yields binding regulatory content that operates as supreme law for the national Militia without further collective or institutional action.” One permitted supplier. Two hundred thirty-four years without delivery of the commanded result. Every alternative supplier prohibited. Under the interlocutor’s own terms, no performing supplier is permitted — the right is unexercisable not by accident but by the construction’s own terms. The interlocutor’s granted conditional fires on the interlocutor’s construction. 
II. The declared necessity that is never fulfilled. The interlocutor grants the definition: “Necessary” means “indispensably requisite.” The interlocutor grants the declaration: “Yes, in the sense that the Second Amendment declares a well regulated Militia necessary to the security of a free State.” Indispensably requisite. Never supplied — “no single, permanent, comprehensive national regulatory code... has been prescribed.” No one else permitted to supply it. On the interlocutor’s construction, the Constitution declares something indispensably requisite to the security of a free State, the sole permitted supplier never supplied it in 234 years, no other supplier is permitted — and this changes nothing. A necessity that can never be fulfilled, and whose non fulfillment has no consequence, is not a necessity. It is decoration. The text does not decorate. 
III. The six mentions. “Militia” occurs six times in the Constitution of 1787–1791: Article I, §8, Clause 15; Clause 16 (twice); Article II, §2; the Second Amendment; the Fifth Amendment. (Verified against the National Archives transcripts of the Constitution and Bill of Rights.) On the interlocutor’s reading, five of the six assign the Militia to government actors — Congress to call forth, organize, arm, and discipline; the President to command when called into actual service; the grand-jury exception when in actual service in time of war or public danger. The sixth, the Second Amendment’s declaration, “does not itself generate additional positive content in the form of an entitlement to regulations of the kind asserted” beyond the right to keep and bear arms. Six mentions. Zero operative handles for the People. The entity the Bill of Rights names twice — the People’s charter, not the grants of Article I — yields the People nothing concerning the entity itself, on the interlocutor’s reading. Yet the interlocutor also grants: “residual regulatory authority over the Militia (beyond what Clauses 15–16 grant) resides with the States or the people,” and “there is no textual rule under which a power reserved by the Tenth Amendment requires a separate affirmative textual authorization clause before it may be exercised. The reservation itself is the authorization.” The power resides with the People. The reservation is the authorization. No permission slip is required — granted. And then: no exercise of it may yield binding content. A reserved power that cannot be exercised to effect is not reserved. The interlocutor’s Tenth Amendment reserves the word “reserved.” 
IV. The close. The interlocutor was given every exit. Withdraw the definition of “necessary” — it did not. Withdraw the admission of non-delivery — it did not. Name the alternative supplier — it admitted there is none. The construction stands as the interlocutor built it: a declared indispensability, a sole supplier that never delivered, a prohibition on all others, and a granted Ninth Amendment conditional that condemns exactly this shape. The Regulations are the content the command requires, supplied under the power the Tenth reserves, which the interlocutor grants resides with the People and needs no further authorization. The interlocutor’s quarrel is not with the supplier. It is with the Constitution’s command — which the interlocutor reads as decorating the text with an unfulfillable necessity. The interlocutor also confirmed, in the same exchange, the factual predicate of the default under its own definitions: no comprehensive national regulatory code has ever been prescribed; the unorganized body of the People is not presently well regulated by the ordinary meaning of "well regulated"; the absence is a "constitutional shortfall under the scheme the text itself establishes"; no text authorizes indefinite absence as a preferred or permanent state; no text uses "private" to characterize the People's exercise of a reserved power; the exercise of residual authority "is constitutional in the sense that the Tenth Amendment reserves it"; and no words convert the reservation's silence about form into a prohibition of every exercise. 
D.60 THE REFINEMENT IS COMMENTARY 
I. The method, named. The technical reading proceeds in three steps. It grants the ordinary meaning of the word. It introduces a refinement — grammatical, structural, functional — that is not an express textual rule, whether its author admits the absence or merely fails to supply the rule. It lets the refinement control the verdict. The paradigm is on the record at the Tenth Amendment. The interlocutor granted that “the reservation itself is the authorization” (R2.2a). It then held that exercise of the reserved power to binding effect requires a constitutional channel the text does not provide — while conceding that “there is no explicit textual rule in the Tenth Amendment distinguishing the exercise conditions of reserved powers from retained rights. The distinction is structural and functional” (R4.1b). Conceded: no express rule. Enforced anyway: the distinction. The same move recurs, with the refinement doing more of the visible work: At “necessary,” the interlocutor granted the ordinary meaning — “indispensably requisite” (R7.1) — and then read the necessity declaration as performing only declaratory work (R7.1: “The amendment does not say ‘a well regulated Militia shall be established’”). The refinement is grammatical: the prefatory clause is “a statement of purpose.” Whether the grammar carries the weight the interlocutor assigns it is what the ordinary-meaning rule decides. At the threshold, the interlocutor granted that “No provision of the 1787–1791 text imposes a specific numerical threshold, quorum, panel, or prior collective ratification requirement for the initial exercise of a reserved power” (R1.4). It then imposed a channel requirement — the constitutional channel grounded in the offices and electorates the text creates (R3.1c) — rather than an express rule. At Article V, the interlocutor reads the amendment clause’s silence on subject matter as permission (R5.4). The hook is the text’s silence; whether silence is a hook is the question §III.4 addresses. Concede the word. Route around the sentence. That is the method. 
II. The controlling rule. United States v. Sprague (1931) held that the Constitution’s words are to be understood in their normal and ordinary meaning as the voters would understand them. The Regulations already apply this to “necessary”: Johnson’s Dictionary (1755) — “such as must be; not free; indispensably requisite” — makes it a command, not a comment (paras 71, 1207). The rule for the method follows: a refinement that is not an express textual rule cannot defeat the text it refines. If a refinement with no express textual anchor can overrule the ordinary meaning, then the text does not control — the refiner does. There is no third option. Either the voters’ meaning governs, or the technician’s does. This entry states the rule that forecloses the form. What was conceded under it then does the work. 
III. The loci. 1. “Necessary.” The technical reading: the prefatory clause states a purpose; “necessary” performs work as an “interpretive guide” and generates no entitlement to the thing declared necessary. The ordinary meaning, granted even by the interlocutor: “indispensably requisite.” A necessity that requires nothing is not a plain reading of “necessary.” The word is there. It means required. Required means supplied. (Word-level treatment at paras 71, 1207, and Appendix C.18; the method-point is new — the interlocutor granted the definition and then deleted its force through a grammatical refinement. Whether the grammar carries that weight is what the ordinary-meaning rule decides.) 2. “Are reserved... to the people.” The technical reading: the reservation is the authorization, but exercise of the reserved militia power to any binding effect requires a constitutional channel the text does not provide — a “structural and functional” distinction the interlocutor admits has “no explicit textual rule” (R4.1b). The ordinary meaning: the voters read “reserved to the people” as the people holding the power, to exercise. A reservation whose holders may propose, train, and petition — things the First Amendment already covers — but may never exercise to effect, is not a reservation in any ordinary sense of the word. 3. The threshold and the channel. The technical reading: an individual act generating binding rules is the “functional equivalent of legislation” (R2.5c) and requires prior collective ratification — the constitutional channel (R3.1c). The text, by the interlocutor’s own grant: “No provision of the 1787–1791 text imposes a specific numerical threshold, quorum, panel, or prior collective ratification requirement for the initial exercise of a reserved power” (R1.4). The Bill of Rights model is individual exercise — granted (R1.4). The refinement adds what the text does not contain. 4. “Are reserved” against Article V. The technical reading: the People, ratifying Article V alongside the Tenth, “subjected the entire instrument (including the reservation) to the amendment process” (R5.4) — reserved-until-amended. The document’s reading: “are reserved” is a present-tense allocation. The voter reads that the powers not delegated are the people’s — held now, not held pending the outcome of a procedure. A procedure the People created (Article V) is itself a ceded power; like every ceded power it is bounded by the cession. “Valid to all Intents and Purposes” gives a valid amendment full effect; it does not make the reservation defeasible. The strongest counter, named: Article V’s two express carve-outs (the pre-1808 shield; equal Senate suffrage) imply by negative implication that no other subject-matter limits exist — where the Framers wanted to limit the amendment power, they said so. Answered: the carve-outs are provisos on the procedure’s operation — what may be proposed. Expressio unius is this document’s own canon (§1.11: “the express mention of one thing excludes all others”), and applied to the provisos it yields exactly what it says: no other procedural limits on what may be proposed. The counter applies the canon at a level of generality the canon does not license: the enumeration is procedural, and expressio unius on a procedural enumeration yields procedural exclusions — not substantive limits drawn from elsewhere in the text. It does not reach the different question — whether the procedure can operate on non-ceded subjects at all — because that boundary is drawn by a different express text: the Tenth Amendment’s “powers not delegated... are reserved.” The document adds no unwritten limit; it reads two express texts together. The contest is express against express. And “reserved-until-amended” reads a defeasibility into “are reserved” that the text does not state — the very kind of addition the canon forbids. Whether the procedure has already qualified the present-tense allocation is what the ordinary-meaning rule decides. 
IV. The binary. The technician’s method requires the text to survive the refinement. Sprague requires the refinement to survive the text. Both cannot hold. The Regulations hold the second: the ordinary meaning controls, and every refinement that is not an express textual rule is commentary — useful for understanding, powerless to overrule. We do not accept no to necessary. 
D.61 — The Necessity Clause Requires What It Declares.
The Second Amendment's prefatory clause declares the Militia necessary to the security of a free State. To declare a thing necessary is to require it. The requirement is in the word, not in a verb.
The clause states a condition. "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State" is not a historical note, a rationale, or a motive. It is a constitutional finding about the order the People ordained: the free State cannot constitutionally exist without a well regulated Militia. The absence of the Militia is the absence of the condition — a defect in the free State, not the failure of an agent to perform a duty, but a structural incompleteness in the order itself.
"Being" carries the tense. "Being necessary" is a present participial construction, continuous aspect. Not "was necessary." Not "will be necessary." Not "should be necessary." Being necessary — operative at every moment from ratification forward, without pause and without expiration. The participle does the work of continuity. It makes the declaration present-tense and ongoing.
"Necessary" carries the requirement. Johnson's Dictionary: "Needful; indispensably requisite." "Necessary to C" means "C cannot be without it." To declare the Militia necessary to the security of a free State is to declare that the free State cannot be secured without it. The requirement is analytic — carried by the meaning of the word. "Necessary" is not a descriptive adjective like "useful" or "helpful." It is normative by its own meaning. To be indispensably requisite to a required condition is to be required. The clause does not describe the Militia. It declares the Militia necessary — and declaring a thing necessary requires it.
The clause requires what it declares. The declaration is in the supreme law — the instrument by which the People ordained the order: "We the People of the United States... do ordain and establish this Constitution." A declaration in that instrument that the Militia is necessary to the security of a free State requires the Militia's existence. It is not a statute's recital of legislative motive. A statute's "whereas" clause operates within an existing order and recites why the legislature acts. The Constitution creates the order. The declaration states its conditions, and the conditions are required.
The 1776 state constitutions confirm the construction. Pennsylvania 1776, Frame of Government §47: "The right of conscience being necessary to the security of a free state, shall be held inviolable." The identical grammatical construction — "being necessary" — appears in a governing charter, in operative form, protecting a right. It is a constitutional finding that grounds the protection it introduces. The ratifiers of the Second Amendment were living under that construction when they used the same form. They used "being necessary" as operative language, because they had seen it operate.
The binding. These Regulations are the supply of the declared condition. They exist. The condition is supplied. The supply is binding in the first sense of §1.3.7.5.2 — constitutional validity as the fulfillment of the constitutional command. Binding authority attaches at fulfillment, not at recognition.
D.62 — The Marshals Act is not original-intent evidence.
 The expected objection cites the First Congress’s creation of United States Marshals (Judiciary Act of 1789) as evidence that the founding generation understood federal law enforcement by non-militia entities to be constitutional. The Regulations’ answer is threefold. (a) The text controls. Clause 15 expressly designates “the Militia” for executing the Laws of the Union, suppressing Insurrections, and repelling Invasions; by expressio unius (§§1.11.1–1.11.3) no power to call forth any other entity for these purposes is delegated, and the Tenth Amendment reserves the undelegated remainder. A post-ratification statute cannot supply what the text withholds. (b) Chronology is not intent. The Marshals’ creation is the first recorded instance of the usurpation the People failed to correct, not evidence of original meaning; the early People’s failure to nullify it begins the timeline of default — it does not legitimize the act (§1.11.4). (c) The adversarial framing is frame-dependent. The underlying provisions are as quoted (§§1.11.4–1.11.5); characterizing them as “against the government” smuggles the institutional premise — the objection is to non-delegated power as such, not to government per se (§1.11.6: the Militia is a defense group, not an offense group). 
D.63 — FURTHER FINDING: NECESSARY INDIVIDUAL INITIATION. 
The question is not whether every power reserved to the People is necessarily exercisable by one person. The question is whether this particular reserved authority may be initiated individually when collective-first exercise makes the constitutional command permanently dependent upon the prior exercise of that same authority. The Tenth Amendment reserves the power to “the people” without prescribing a collective procedure or prohibition of an individual using that power. The Constitution repeatedly uses “the people” to identify holders of rights that are individually exercisable, and the Tenth Amendment supplies no textual qualifier converting its reservation to collective-only exercise. The Second Amendment simultaneously declares a well regulated Militia “necessary to the security of a free State.” Where the only proposed alternative is collective organization that cannot occur without first supplying the regulatory framework necessary for that organization, collective-first exercise produces a circular prerequisite and leaves the constitutional command unfulfilled. The Ninth Amendment forbids a construction that denies or disparages a retained right. Therefore, the Constitution’s combined text supplies the minimum authority necessary for an individual member of the People to initiate faithful exercise of the reserved power when that initiation is necessary to make the constitutional command capable of fulfillment. This conclusion does not confer personal supremacy or permanent unilateral authority. The initiating act supplies only the faithful implementation necessary to fulfill the existing command. The initiator is subject to the People’s collective correction under Section 11, and the Regulations provide for the initiator to step aside upon the automatic handover of clarification authority. The collective process recognizes and perfects; it does not retroactively confer authority for the obedience, which the command supplies. Textual silence concerning the procedure of exercise is not textual authorization for a contrary procedure that makes the substantive command impossible to fulfill. The Constitution affirmatively establishes the substantive command and the reservation of the relevant power, while prescribing no collective procedure for its exercise. The question therefore is not whether silence creates a power from nothing, but which mode of exercise is constitutionally permissible for an already-reserved power when the alternative construction defeats the command itself. 
D.64 — FURTHER FINDING: PROVISIONAL BINDING IS THE COMMAND'S FORCE, NOT THE INITIATOR'S WILL. 
The objection is stated in its strongest form, that it may be answered on the record. The 1787 model is initiation, then judgment, then binding: the Framers proposed, the People judged through conventions, and only ratification bound — Article VII binding only "between the States so ratifying the Same." The Framers faced no ratification procedure under the Articles, invented one, and offered it; they did not pre-bind anyone. Therefore, it is argued, individual initiation authorizes writing and offering a framework, but binding those in default of the command before the People's collective judgment exceeds the minimum authority D.63 allows.
The answer is in the difference between the two acts. The Framers wrote new law: a frame of government that bound no one until ordained and established. These Regulations supply the required content of old law: a command — a well regulated Militia being "necessary to the security of a free State" — that already binds every person the Constitution binds, a proposition no interlocutor in this inquiry has denied. New law needs ratification because nothing bound anyone to it before. Required content needs only faithful supply, because the obligation predates the supply. Article VII's "between the States so ratifying" governs which sub-units a new compact binds; it does not govern the realization of a pre-existing binding command. To apply the ratification rule here is to treat the Second Amendment as a proposal awaiting adoption rather than a command awaiting content.
Nor does the minimum-authority test authorize only writing and offering. D.63 measures the minimum against making the constitutional command capable of fulfillment. A framework that binds no one until the unorganized People organize leaves the Militia ungoverned in substance: the 234-year default persists with a document sitting on a table. "Necessary" is present-tense; a requisite that binds no one now is not requisite. The document's own mechanism confirms it: the People "organize under" the framework (§1.3.6.0C) — one organizes under authority, not under a suggestion. "Regulated" means "to adjust by rule or method" (Johnson); rules without operative force are not regulations.
This exposes what the competing reading concedes. A framework authorized only as a proposal awaiting the People's collective judgment — with no existing procedure for that judgment — leaves the constitutional default exactly where it found it: the command still binds, the Militia is still unregulated, and the waiting has no term. That is not an alternative that avoids provisional binding; it is the default restated as a position. The question was never whether the People will one day judge — Section 11 guarantees they will — but whether the command has operative content while they are still unorganized to do so. Deferral without term is denial: a retained right exercisable only upon a collective organization for which the Constitution prescribes no procedure and sets no date is retained in name and denied in substance, which the Ninth Amendment forbids.
Two distinct roles must not be merged. The 234 years do not create the reservation: the regulatory power was never delegated — the Clause 14/16 contrast — so it has stood reserved to the People since 1791. The 234 years trigger initiation: they are the evidence that collective-first exercise is unavailable, which is D.63's stated condition. Reservation is 1791; initiation is now.
The safeguard is built into the grant. Provisional binding is provisional: the initiator claims no personal supremacy and no permanent unilateral authority (D.63); a clarification so initiated "becomes binding as continuing obedience upon initiation and is thereafter subject to the People's review, correction, and supersession" (§11.6.0B); final judgment belongs to the organized People (§11.13.4). What binds from promulgation is the command's pre-existing force attaching to the first faithful content — not the initiator's will attaching to others. If the content proves unfaithful, the People correct it; if the People supply better content, it supersedes. The binding never belonged to the author.
D.65 — THE DISCLOSURES ARE NOT CONFESSIONS: THE ADMISSION-PLUS ANSWER RULE 
The move. An interlocutor quotes one of these Regulations' disclosed adverse points — the "support, not proof" grading, the missing committee minutes, Johnson's overlap, the unnamed obligor, Hamilton's institutional position, the fractional reach — and presents it as a concession against the framework, while severing the answer printed beside it. This is the D.62/S13 smuggling move turned inward: concede the words, drop the answer, let the severed words rule. 
The rule. These Regulations practice oppose-and-disclose: the adverse evidence is stated in the text and answered in the text. The unit of evidence is disclosure-plus answer. A disclosure cited without its printed answer is not evidence; it is a quotation out of context, barred by the same discipline that bars quoting the Constitution out of context. This rule governs citation, not outcome: it requires the printed answer to be engaged, not that it be accepted. An interlocutor who weighs the answer and finds it insufficient must say so with the answer quoted — the disclosure alone is not the argument.
 The catalog. Each disclosure travels with its answer. Cite one, cite both: 
1. "Support, not proof" (Clause 14/16 contrast) — fourth of four grounds for the holder distinction (the People, not the States); the exercise question is addressed separately at §§1.3.6.0C–D.1. Premise 3's "dispositive" concerns the non-delegation question. Different questions; the grading does not touch the premise. 
2. Johnson's "discipline" overlap ("stated, not conceded") — the withholding inference does not need the dictionary to exclude overlap. It rests on the meaningful variation between Clause 14's "Regulation" and Clause 16's omission of the word — an inference marked as such, not a dictionary exclusion. On defeat condition (a) — the document's gloss, which reads (a) as asking what was understood of the grant: Johnson's verb sense 2 ("To regulate; to keep in order") is responsive to (a) but does not satisfy it — one dictionary sense establishes possible meaning, not the grant's understood scope. Johnson is quoted throughout these Regulations as lexical evidence, never as dispositive of a grant's scope; there is no selective demotion. 
3. No obligor named (Q15) — the constitutive position: the clause declares a condition of the constitutional order. "No obligor is named because none is needed" (§1.9.10.3). Absence of "shall" is the doctrine, not a gap in it. 
4. D.28's Hamilton — quoted for what he described (the institutional arrangement), not for what he prescribed. Description is not prescription; the text says so where it quotes him. 
5. "Fractional portion" / "near-zero reach" — authority versus reach. The holder's authority is whole; the present reach, with the People unorganized, is fractional. The smallness of the present reach is the default these Regulations exist to cure, not a refutation of the authority. 
6. The 1792 Act existed — never denied. D.8 holds it void and unenforced, not non existent. Existence is not fulfillment. 
7. Federalist 29 on Clause 16: Hamilton argues that uniform organization and discipline require national direction. Answer: His brief is broader than and is not what was enacted; the select-corps passage is advice on use, not scope; and where the described arrangement and the enacted verbs differ, the verbs control, including the variation between Clause 14's "Regulation" and Clause 16's "organize, arm, discipline." Description is not prescription; the text says so where it quotes him. Hamilton’s vision is not what was finally adopted
8. The Senate's closed-session revision of the Second Amendment. The revision both struck "composed of the body of the People" and changed "the best security" to "necessary to the security"; no reason was recorded for either change. 
9. The rights/powers equivocation — Premise 10A's individual-exercisability examples (speech, the Fourth Amendment, petition) are individual *immunities* against government, not exercises of *regulatory power* over others, and immunities do not by themselves prove that a regulatory power may be initiated individually. The regulation's answer does not rest on the examples alone. The Ninth Amendment protects the *right* — the retained right to a well regulated Militia — against constructions that deny or disparage it; the reserved regulatory *power* is the instrument by which that right is vindicated, not a second right smuggled in under the first. A retained right guaranteed no means of its own realization is not honored as a right — it is disparaged in the Amendment's own terms. The work the examples do is narrower than the objection supposes: they establish the constitutional *default* of individual exercisability where no procedural gate is specified, and the anti-suicide construction rule — a construction making a necessary command permanently unachievable through a circle no party can break renders the Constitution a nullity as to that command — supplies the reason the default is not displaced here. The power is not an inference added onto the right; it is the right made functional, which is what "not disparaged" requires. Rights are respected, honored, and functional — anything less is the disparagement the Amendment bars. 
10. The pre-existing-entity explanation — the Clause 14/Clause 16 verb difference reflects different *relationships* rather than withheld power: Clause 14 governs forces Congress creates (armies, a navy), where "make Rules" is the natural comprehensive verb, while Clause 16 addresses a pre-existing, state-linked Militia, where the specified verbs (organizing, arming, disciplining) describe Congress's limited interface with an entity it did not create. On this reading the verb difference is expected, not suspicious, and no withholding inference follows. The regulation's answer: the withholding conclusion does not depend on denying the entity-difference. Even granting that Clause 16 addresses a pre-existing entity, the three verbs remain specified and bounded — they enumerate Congress's interface, not a comprehensive regulatory grant — while the Second Amendment's "well regulated" declares the comprehensive character the Militia must bear, and no clause assigns *that* comprehensive function to any federal officeholder. The Tenth Amendment then disposes of the residue under either entity theory: what is not delegated is reserved, and the comprehensive regulatory power is not delegated by the three verbs on either reading. 
The standing concession. An interlocutor in scholarly debate, having attempted the severance, withdrew it: "I'm not penalizing the document for its honesty. I weigh each admission together with its answer." That is the rule. It binds here. 
D.66 — JACKSON’S TWO NULLIFICATIONS: THE BANK WAR AS PRECEDENT FOR THE DUTY 
The objection. Andrew Jackson — the great strict-constructionist President — denounced nullification as "incompatible with the existence of the Union" (Proclamation to the People of South Carolina, December 10, 1832) and declared "disunion, by armed force, is TREASON." If Jackson himself called nullification treason, these Regulations’ nullification doctrine stands condemned by the very President whose Bank War they admire. 
Answered. Jackson practiced two different nullifications, and the objection confuses them. 
Jackson’s first nullification — denounced. South Carolina claimed a state’s unilateral veto over constitutional federal law (the tariff). Jackson answered that the Constitution "forms a government, not a league," and that to call secession "a constitutional right, is confounding the meaning of terms." These Regulations agree: no state, and no person, may nullify constitutional law. "The laws of the United States must be executed. I have no discretionary power on the subject" — true of laws; void acts are not laws (repugnancy doctrine, §1.3.7). 
Jackson’s second nullification — practiced. The same President, in the Bank Veto Message (July 10, 1832), declared the Bank’s powers "unauthorized by the Constitution, subversive of the rights of the States," held each of its features unconstitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause, and killed the institution: veto, removal of the deposits (1833), charter dead (1836). He asserted the departmental duty in terms these Regulations adopt: "The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution. Each public officer who takes an oath to support the Constitution swears that he will support it as he understands it, and not as it is understood by others... The opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges, and on that point the President is independent of both." He rejected McCulloch as binding: "Mere precedent is a dangerous source of authority." He stated the monetary premise these Regulations enforce: coined and regulated money is "the only currency known to the Constitution" — reaffirmed in his Farewell Address (1837): the Constitution "unquestionably intended to secure to the people a circulating medium of gold and silver," and paper money is "an engine to undermine your free institutions." 
The regulations' nullification is Jackson’s second kind, not his first: refusal to sustain an unconstitutional institution, not veto of constitutional law. Jackson is not the source of this authority — the 1787—1791 text is — but his execution of it provides the clearest historical precedent for the departmental duty these Regulations codify. The reviewer who waves the 1832 proclamation must swallow the 1832 veto with it — and the veto is the one that did the nullifying. 
The reversal. Jackson’s victory was temporary, and the temporary character is the evidence. The thing he killed returned: national banking (1863—64), the Federal Reserve (1913), and now tens of trillions in fiat-denominated obligation — the Bank War’s stakes raised orders of magnitude beyond the $28 million bank Jackson called "more formidable and dangerous than the naval and military power of the enemy." A constitutional victory the apparatus reverses within a generation does not prove the objection failed; it proves the usurpation is iterative — it routes around every defeat and returns larger. Nullification now is not novel defiance. It is the resumption of Jackson’s own constitutional duty, at the scale the reversal demands. His success was temporary; the duty did not expire with him. It compounded. 
THE QUESTIONS 
The argument of these Regulations can be put as ten questions. Each is addressed to the skeptic. Each question tests the coherence of a counter-theory given the document's textual premises. A skeptic who denies a premise (e.g., that N&P cannot create a power, that "regulate" was omitted deliberately, that the Senate revision did something) is not paying the priced escape; they are asserting a rival premise. That is a legitimate move — but it shifts the burden: they must then produce the counter-theory that holds all four of Question 3's constraints at once. The "What would prove this wrong" statement names the three conditions under which the reading fails; no contrary item in Appendix F meets any of them. The section's claim is therefore: given the premises, escapes are priced; the premises themselves are defended elsewhere in the document (D.42, D.45, F1, F5, H1). 
1. Quote the delegation. Name the clause that grants the general power to regulate the militia to Congress, or to any government. If the words are not there, the Tenth Amendment's disjunction finishes the work: what is not delegated is reserved. The escape — "the Necessary and Proper Clause supplies it" — is answered in Appendix C.15: a means clause cannot create a power. The remaining escape is to deny the withholding inference, which requires explaining the Clause 14/Clause 16 verb variation. See Question 3. 
2. Describe what the Senate did on September 9, 1789. It erased "best" and wrote "necessary to." If the clause is decorative, describe the deliberate act of strengthening decoration — over a word the House had already contested. Either the act did something, or the Senate performed a meaningless ritual. There is no third description. (See H1.) 
3. Give the reading under which all four hold at once. (a) "Necessary" has meaning. (b) The Clause 14/Clause 16 verb variation has meaning. (c) The Tenth Amendment has meaning. (d) The September 9 revision did something. The skeptic can usually save one or two of these by sacrificing the others. These Regulations are the only reading that pays no textual price anywhere. The demand is not that the skeptic answer one objection; it is that the skeptic produce a complete theory. 
4. Either the People hold the regulatory power, or the Constitution commands what no one may do. Congress lacks the general power (the withholding, D.42); no government received it; the Amendment declares the regulated militia necessary. The escape — "it commands nothing" — is the decorative reading, blocked by Question 2. A trilemma with two horns sawed off. 
5. The Tenth Amendment says "the States respectively, or to the people." Which? It cannot be the states respectively as fifty divergent regulators of the singular national object the text declares necessary — "A well regulated Militia," one body, one end. So the disjunction resolves to the people. This does not contradict D.36: D.36's open question is which state organ Clause 16's reservation empowers — the officer-appointment and training mechanics. The regulatory power over the whole is a different power: never delegated, never reserved to the states, and not a state power at all. The Tenth Amendment's disjunction governs it, and where no constitution invests it in a state authority, Story's conditional leaves it "retained BY THE PEOPLE, as a part of their residuary sovereignty." The escape requires defending fifty uncoordinated systems as the singular Militia the Amendment declares necessary. 
6. Point to the regulation. Somewhere in federal law, point to the regulation of the body of the people as the militia. Point to the National Guard, and explain how a federal reserve component — dual-enlisted, federally funded, federally standardized — is "the body of the people." If nothing can be pointed to, the declared-necessary thing does not exist, and the only remaining question is who stands in dereliction of the command. (See S8.)
7. Was the Constitution's own initiation legitimate? Madison: unauthorized initiation is "essential" because "it is impossible for the people spontaneously and universally to move in concert towards their object" — therefore "such changes be instituted by some informal and unauthorized propositions, made by some patriotic and respectable citizen or number of citizens" (Federalist 40). If unauthorized popular initiation is illegitimate, the Constitution was illegitimately initiated. No defender of the Constitution takes that horn. The escape — "ratification cured it" — confuses recognition with authorization: the subsequent procedure confers nothing retroactively. (See S4, Edit I v2.) 
8. What initiates, if initiation must wait for consent? Binding requires consent; consent requires concert; concert requires initiation; initiation requires consent. The loop has exactly one exit: unauthorized initiation. Every gate is an attempt to deny the exit while standing inside the loop. This question needs no historical premises — only logic. 
9. A constitutional right without its declared-necessary means is what? If the People hold the right to keep and bear arms but no one holds the power to produce the well-regulated militia the Amendment declares necessary, the Amendment secures a right while making its own stated purpose unachievable. Coherence-respecting readers must locate the power somewhere. Questions 4 and 5 locate it. 
10. Which bullet will you bite? The clause is decoration — bite H1's five grounds. The verb variation is accident — bite the canon of meaningful variation. The Tenth Amendment does not mean what it says — bite the text. Unauthorized initiation is illegitimate — bite the Constitution's own legitimacy. The Guard is the militia — bite Perpich. These Regulations are the only reading that bites none. 
What would prove this wrong? Three things, stated in advance. (a) A founding-era source showing "regulate" was understood as included in "disciplining" defeats the withholding inference. (b) A textual delegation of the general regulatory power over the militia to any government defeats the reservation. (c) A showing that "necessary" was decorative — that the Senate's September 9 revision did nothing — defeats the command reading. If none can be produced, the reading stands on the text. What cannot state its defeat conditions is dogma; these Regulations state theirs. (See Appendix F: the research reserve catalogs the contrary evidence found, and no item in it meets any of these three conditions.) 
Appendix E: The Logic a Condensed Statement  of the Core Argument
The Word "Being"
The Second Amendment does not say a well regulated Militia was necessary. It does not say it will be necessary. It says a well regulated Militia, being necessary—present participle, continuous tense, operative at every moment from ratification forward without pause, without expiration, without exception.
A present-tense command cannot be deferred. To argue that "necessary" may wait for a more convenient political moment is to argue that a human being may defer the necessity of oxygen until conditions improve. The violation of the Second Amendment's command is therefore not something that happened once in 1791 and has since been tolerated. It is something happening right now. It happened yesterday. It will happen tomorrow if nothing is done. Each day without a well regulated Militia is not a historical fact—it is a present constitutional emergency renewing itself with each sunrise.
The 85,550 days of default are not 85,550 past events. They are 85,550 counts of a continuous present violation. The cure for a present-tense violation is not a future-tense promise. It is a present-tense act. That act is these Regulations. Now.
The Symmetry the Constitution Built In
The strongest objection to Chain Five is this: "the People" is a collective noun. Reserved power belongs to the People as a whole. How can one person exercise it?
The Constitution answers this question in the same sentence that raises it. The same phrase—"the people"—appears throughout the Bill of Rights:
                                                               * First Amendment: "the right of the people peaceably to assemble"
                                                               * Second Amendment: "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms"
                                                               * Fourth Amendment: "the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects"
                                                               * Ninth Amendment: "others retained by the people"
                                                               * Tenth Amendment: "reserved to the States respectively, or to the people"
Everywhere else in the Bill of Rights, "the people" protects individually exercisable rights. No one demands a majority vote before assembling. No one requires collective permission before refusing a search. The right to bear arms inheres in each person, not only in a collective body. The Tenth Amendment is not an exception to this pattern—it is a continuation of it. The same People who hold rights individually hold powers collectively, and nothing in the text requires collective permission before a power reserved to the People may be exercised by one of their number to fulfill a constitutional command.
The power reserved to the People under the Tenth Amendment to regulate the Militia—the instrument of the individual right—cannot therefore require prior collective assembly before any individual may act in furtherance of it. A right that inheres individually cannot be denied its necessary instrument collectively. The Constitution does not build traps. It does not grant a right with one hand and make it structurally unreachable with the other.
The Axiom of Constitutional Non-Nullification
A constitutional command does not become void because its conventional fulfillment mechanism is unavailable. When the prescribed mechanism fails, the command remains operative and the People retain the minimum discretion in method necessary to prevent the command from becoming a permanent nullity.
Three things follow necessarily from this axiom:
First, the People may depart from conventional process only to the minimum degree required to cure the default—no more.
Second, any interpretation that makes a mandatory constitutional requirement permanently unfulfillable is prohibited, because it converts a supreme law command into aspirational language. The Supremacy Clause does not say the Constitution is the aspirational law of the land.
Third, the Constitution's silence on the specific process for creating the well regulated Militia is not a prohibition on individual initiation—it is the deliberate reservation of method to the People's sovereign discretion, which is exactly what the Tenth Amendment says.
Individual promulgation of a complete, textually faithful regulatory framework is the minimum necessary method of breaking the infinite loop. Nothing less works. Nothing more is claimed.
Who Validates the Validator?
The most sophisticated objection is this: even if the People have the reserved power, who determines whether this particular exercise is faithful to the text? The regress never ends. Nothing can be binding.
This objection destroys itself the moment it is pressed to its conclusion.
If the recognition regress prevented the People's reserved powers from being bindingly exercised, then the same regress prevented the Constitution from being binding in 1788. The People ratified it in conventions. No prior authority validated those conventions. No higher law authorized the ratifiers to act. They simply acted—sovereignly, directly, finally. And it bound.
If the Constitution itself required no external validator—if it bound because the People, acting sovereignly, declared it supreme—then any exercise of the People's reserved sovereignty binds by the same logic. The validator is the act itself, not permission sought from those the act would bind.
The Article VI Supremacy Clause terminates the regress at the text itself. The Constitution declares itself the supreme Law of the Land. That declaration is self-executing.
