It does not say it becomes supreme when enough people recognize it. Supremacy is declared. Authority flows from the text downward, not from recognition upward.
The standard for whether these Regulations are faithful to the text is the text—available to every person, every court, every official, every artificial intelligence that can read. No additional authority is required. The question is not "who approves this." It is "does this faithfully fulfill what the Constitution commands." If it does, it binds.
Any entity that denies the binding status of these Regulations on the grounds that they have not been "recognized" must answer: by what authority was the Constitution itself recognized as binding in 1788? If the answer is "by the sovereign act of the People," then these Regulations, as a sovereign act of the People fulfilling a constitutional command, are binding for the identical reason. If the answer is anything else, the respondent has abandoned popular sovereignty, and with it, the entire constitutional order they are claiming to defend.
The People’s property, Protected All the Way Through
One practical objection to the monetary restoration is that a sudden transition from fiat currency to gold and silver could harm ordinary people through disruption.
This objection misreads the Regulations. The farmer accepted Federal Reserve notes because he had no legal alternative. But those notes were void ab initio—invalid from their inception under Article I, Section 10's command that only gold and silver coin may serve as tender. The system that forced them on him owes restitution, not the other way around.
The obligation to make citizens whole flows from the institutional instrumentalities of the violation—the Federal Reserve System, the Treasury's fiat issuance apparatus, the financial entities that accumulated benefit from the unconstitutional system—not from the citizens who held void currency in good faith. The farmer's good faith creates no liability for him. It creates maximum restitution obligation against the system that gave him no other choice.
Furthermore, the right to continuous access to one's own property during a constitutional transition is itself a retained right under the Ninth Amendment. The transition sequence is therefore constitutionally required to proceed as follows: citizen property is protected with no gap in access; institutional seizure proceeds in parallel; seized assets are converted and distributed; void fiat instruments are retired, constitutional money fully circulates. Step five never precedes step one. 
These Regulations do not harm the farmer, the widow, or the single mother. They end the harm those three have been suffering for their entire lives. The restitution flows toward them. the liability runs against the system that did the extracting. This is not a disruption. It is the end of the disruption that has been running for over a century.


What Cannot Be Denied
After everything above, the argument against these Regulations is reduced to denying one of the following:
                                                               * The Constitution means what it says.
                                                               * The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution self-authorizing.
                                                               * The Ninth Amendment prohibits constructions that make constitutional rights self-defeating.
                                                               * The Tenth Amendment actually reserves powers to the People.
                                                               * Individual constitutional rights are self-executing.
None of those is a legal argument. Each one is a denial of the Constitution itself. Any critic who goes there has not defeated the logic. They have demonstrated that they are not operating under the Constitution as written.
The grammar is settled. The axiom is stated. The symmetry holds. The regress is closed. The farmer is protected through to the end.
The logic is complete. The command is satisfied. The free state is secured.
Appendix F: Historical Research Reserve 
A note on contrary material. Every item below that cuts against these Regulations' reading is included by design — so that no reader discovers an undisclosed weakness. Each such item carries its answer at the location cited beside it. And none of them meets the defeat conditions: no item in this reserve shows "regulate" was understood as included in "disciplining," none produces a textual delegation of the general regulatory power over the militia to any government, and none shows the Senate's September 9 revision did nothing. The contrary evidence is answered; it does not defeat the reading. (See "The Questions.") 


F.1 Purpose and status. This appendix is a research record, not an argument. It collects the founding-era historical material surveyed in these Regulations' preparation — newspaper items, Convention records, state-constitution texts, the federal enactment ledger, and modern scholarship — with each item's source status stated plainly. Supporting and contrary findings are both recorded; the contrary findings are included by design, so that no reader discovers an undisclosed weakness. Items not verified against originals are labeled as such, and open research items are marked open. Nothing in this appendix alters the Regulations, which stand on the constitutional text; this material is supporting evidence only. Deliberate placement — the record. "Well regulated" does not appear among Congress's Article I militia verbs — to organize, arm, discipline, call forth, and govern when employed (Clauses 15–16) — and "regulate" is not among them. "Well regulated" appears instead in the Second Amendment: a provision of the Bill of Rights, the charter the People demanded as the condition of ratification and ratified as their own. The regulatory end was lodged with the People, not with Congress. The deliberateness is confirmed by a rejection, not a proposal — and the rejection is militia-specific. On June 18, 1787, Alexander Hamilton — the Convention's most expansive voice for national power — proposed, in Article XI of his plan, that "the Militia of all the states [be] under the sole and exclusive direction of the United States, the officers of which to be appointed and commissioned by them." The plan was never debated, voted on, or referred to committee. On June 19 the Convention postponed the New Jersey Plan and voted to proceed on the Virginia Plan as preferable - which as a practical matter shelved Hamilton's plan without any vote on it. William Samuel Johnson's remark on June 21 - "praised by everybody" but "supported by none" (Madison's notes, Farrand I:363) — records its reception.  What the Convention then wrote answers Hamilton's Article XI on its own terms: Clause 16 reserves "to the States respectively, the Appointment of the Officers." The verb question belongs to the August record: Mason's three "regulate" formulations of August 18 were none of them adopted in that form, and the enacted text omits "regulate" (see F.4). What was not adopted does not govern — but the non-adoption is itself the adopted fact. Honest note, marked as inference: that the Convention deliberately withheld plenary national direction of the militia is inference from the Article XI-to-Clause 16 reversal; what is text is the absence in Article I and the presence in the Second Amendment, and what is adopted history is the June 19 vote to proceed on the Virginia Plan (shelving Hamilton's plan without a vote on it) and the August verb record. (Answered in D.28; see F.4.)  


F.2 "Necessary" in founding-era usage: the duty-command context. Henry Knox to George Washington, January 18, 1790, War Office, New York: "First. That it is the indispensable duty of every nation, to establish all necessary institutions for its own perfection and defence." "Secondly. That it is a Capital security to a free state, for the great body of the people to possess a Competent knowledge of the military art." "Fourthly. That every man of the proper age and ability of body, is firmly bound by the social compact, to perform, personally, his proportion of military duty for the defence of the state." "Fifthly. That all men of the legal military age, should be armed, enrolled, and held responsible for different degrees of military service." "And Sixthly. That, agreeably to the Constitution, the United States are to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia; and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States; reserving to the States respectively, the appointment of the Officers, and the authority of training the militia according to the discipline prescribed by Congress" "An energetic national militia is to be regarded as the Capital security of a free republic; and not a standing army, forming a distinct class in the community." "But the people of the United States will cheerfully consent to the expenses of a measure calculated to serve as a perpetual barrier to their liberties"  
This is the strongest single item: a sitting Secretary of War, in an official 1790 plan, uses "necessary" inside an explicit duty formulation, pairs the militia with "Capital security to a free state," asserts every able man "firmly bound by the social compact" to personal military duty, and asserts the United States "are to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia" — public arming at federal expense. Caveat: this proves Knox's usage and the administration's position, not newspaper reception or the Second Amendment's ratified meaning; newspaper republication or reception of the plan was not located (F.10). 
Contrary nuance — the same verified primary. In the same document Knox uses "necessary"/"necessity" contingently:  "It is the introduction and diffusion of vice and corruption of manners into the mass of the people, that renders a standing army necessary."  "...even philosophers, and the advocates for liberty, have frequently confessed their use and necessity, in certain cases." (of standing armies) 
The word carried its ordinary range, including "required by circumstances." The document's "necessary = now" thesis therefore rests on the constitutional-command context, not on the bare word (see H1). 
Further usages (secondary-reported; originals not checked): George Washington to James Madison, February 5, 1788 — "conceiving it of indispensable necessity" (political urgency, not constitutional command); Preston, Connecticut, town-meeting instructions, November 26, 1787 — militia provisions described as "usual and necessary for citizens of a free country." Excluded: an item attributed to "Brutus," New York Journal, October 25, 1787 ("It was absolutely necessary to carry arms for fear of pirates...") — attribution and context look suspicious against the known Brutus essays; flagged as unverified and not cited. 


F.3 Ratification-era newspaper treatment of Congress's militia powers. "Centinel," Philadelphia Independent Gazetteer — contrary (secondary-reported, cross-verified in two independent secondary sources with identical wording; original newspaper image not checked — see F.7): > "It is remarkable that this article only makes the observation, 'that a well regulated militia, composed of the body of the people, is the best security of a free state;' it does not ordain, or constitutionally provide for, the establishment of such a one. The absolute command vested by other sections in Congress over the militia, are not in the least abridged by this amendment. The militia may still be subjected to martial law..., may still be marched from state to state and made the unwilling instruments of crushing the last efforts of expiring liberty." This is the most important contrary item in the survey on two independent points: (1) a prominent Anti-Federalist expressly reads the militia clause as non-commanding — "it does not ordain" — directly opposing the document's H1 fifth ground; (2) the same writer describes Congress's Clause 16 authority as "absolute command... over the militia," conceding the federal regulatory power the document holds was never ceded. The document answers (1) in H1's Centinel paragraph and (2) in D.28 (see F1). Date discrepancy flagged: one compilation dates the piece July 2, 1789; the law-review pinpoint dates "Centinel, Revived, No. XXIX" to September 9, 1789 — the same day the Senate altered the amendment's wording. The passage quotes the House version ("best security"), so a September 9 date remains chronologically coherent, but neither date should be asserted without checking the original issue. Hamilton, Federalist No. 29 (Daily Advertiser, January 10, 1788) — contrary (primary, located — Founders Online; full page not re-opened): > "What reasonable cause of apprehension can be inferred from a power in the Union to prescribe regulations for the militia and to command its services when necessary...?" Fuller verified passages (Avalon Project): "THE power of regulating the militia, and of commanding its services in times of insurrection and invasion are natural incidents to the duties of superintending the common defense"; "confiding the regulation of the militia to the direction of the national authority"; "If a well-regulated militia be the most natural defense of a free country, it ought certainly to be under the regulation and at the disposal of that body which is constituted the guardian of the national security"; "a power in the Union to prescribe regulations for the militia, and to command its services when necessary, while the particular States are to have the SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS." A leading framer publicly presented "regulations for the militia" as a federal power in 1788, pairing "regulations" with "when necessary." Answered in D.28 (see F1). George Mason, Virginia ratifying convention, June 14, 1788 — mixed (secondary-reported, search excerpt; Elliot cite not re-verified): > "The general government ought, at the same time, to have some such power. But we need not give them power to abolish our militia. If they neglect to arm them, and prescribe proper discipline, they will be of no use." Mason concedes "the general government ought... to have some such power," while treating congressional neglect to arm and discipline as breach of an expected duty. Double-edged: supports the document's duty/neglect analysis; assumes the power's grant. (See D.43.) Tench Coxe ("a Pennsylvanian"), Pennsylvania Gazette, January 7, 1788 — support (secondary reported): > "Congress have no power to disarm the militia. Their swords, and every other terrible implement of the soldier, are the birthright of an American. . . . [T]he unlimited power of the sword is not in the hands of either the federal or state governments, but, where I trust in God it will ever remain, in the hands of the people." A Federalist advocate publicly lodging the sword-power "in the hands of the people" rather than either government — the closest period-newspaper analogue to the retained-power thesis. Note: Coxe denies the power to disarm, not the Clause 16 regulatory power as such. "One of the People," Federal Gazette (Philadelphia), June 18, 1789 — support (secondary-reported): > "Let these truths sink deep into our hearts: that the people are the masters of their rulers and that rulers are the servants of the people... and that a master reserves to himself the exclusive care of all that property, and of every thing else which he has not committed to the care of those servants." A crisp master/servant reserved-powers statement during the amendments debate: whatever was "not committed to the care of those servants" is reserved. Supports the reservation framework; does not name the militia power specifically. New York ratifying convention, July 7, 1788 — support (secondary-reported; quotation recorded with ellipsis as in the compilation): > "no regulations tending to render the general militia useless and defenceless... ought to be made" A ratifying convention using "regulations" in a prohibitory, duty-like sense: regulations must not destroy the militia. Further citizen-soldier items (secondary-reported; none verified against originals): "John DeWitt," Boston American Herald, November 1, 1787 — "a well regulated militia, composed of the yeomanry of the country have ever been considered as the bulwark of a free society..."; "the Republican," Connecticut Courant, December 3, 1787 — "every citizen is required by law to be a soldier; we are marshaled into companies, regiments, and brigades for the defence of our country"; "Philodemos," Pennsylvania Gazette, March 5, 1788 — "Every free man has a right to the use of the press, so he has to the use of his arms"; "MT. Cicero," State Gazette of South Carolina, March 8, 1788 — "No free government was ever founded, or ever preserved in its liberty, without uniting the characters of the citizen and soldier in those destined for the defence of the state..."; Rev. Nicholas Collin ("Foreign Spectator"), Pennsylvania Gazette, September 8, 1788 — "While the people have property, arms in their hands, and only a spark of a noble spirit, the most corrupt congress must be mad to form any project of tyranny"; Tench Coxe ("a Pennsylvanian"), Federal Gazette, November 7, 1788 — "the people are confirmed by the next article [the Second Amendment] in their right to keep and bear their private arms"; Gazette of the United States (New York), September 9, 1789 (extract of a Fayetteville, North Carolina letter — date anomaly: the letter is dated September 12, 1789, after the issue; likely a compilation typo, flagged) — "The right of the people to keep and bear arms has been recognized by the General Government; but the best security of that right after all is that military spirit, that taste for martial exercises, which has always distinguished the free citizens of these States...."; Providence Gazette & Country Journal, January 8, 1790 — "...that the right of the citizens to bear arms in defence of themselves and the State, and to assemble peaceably together... shall not be questioned." Clause 14/Clause 16 wording contrast: no newspaper item was located that explicitly contrasts Clause 14's "make Rules" language with Clause 16's "regulate" wording. That contrast remains the document's own textual observation, without located period-newspaper discussion. 


F.4 The Convention record on "regulate" (supports D.28; see F1 for the proposal text). Mason's three "regulate" motions, Convention floor, August 18, 1787 (verified against Madison's notes, Avalon Project): (1) "a power to regulate the militia"; (2) "to make laws for the regulation and discipline of the militia of the several States reserving to the States the appointment of the officers"; (3) "to make laws for regulating and disciplining the militia, not exceeding one tenth part in any one year." None was adopted in that form — the enacted text omits "regulate." The Convention heard the maximal reading and divided the power anyway: Madison — regulation "naturally appertaining to the authority charged with the public defence" and "not in its nature to be divisible between two distinct authorities"; Ellsworth — Mason's motion "went too far"; Sherman seconded; Dickinson — "the States never would nor ought to give up all authority over the Militia." This Convention-record material is on the document's side. Story, Commentaries §§1196, 1199–1202 (verified against the 1833 first edition, Wikisource): §1196 adopts Hamilton's "natural incident" language nearly verbatim; §1200 supplies Convention-record evidence — the clause "was subsequently referred to a committee, who reported in favour of the power; and after considerable discussion it was adopted in its present shape by a decided majority... passed by a vote of nine states against two"; §1202 records the founding generation's own answer as concurrent state power on congressional neglect — state fallback, not popular action. Honest note (recorded, not evaded): the broad construction — Hamilton's affirmative-grant reading — was the majority contemporary reading (Story; Tucker on organizing/disciplining, D.38; Mason's assumption of the grant, D.43; the First Congress's 1792 exercise, D.41). The document does not claim the narrow reading prevailed in 1788; it claims the enacted text bounds the grant to its verbs, and no majority of commentators can confer a power the text withholds (answered in D.28; see F1). Still open: Mason's June 14, 1788 Elliot 3:380 quotation not re-verified; Virginia fallback amendment item 11 text not re-verified; Tucker 1803 full text taken on the proposal's word; D.36's Story conditional — a find on Story ch. 22 returned no match, likely from another chapter, unverified. 


F.5 The state-constitutions survey record (supports D.45; see F6 for the proposal text). Universe: the founding-era constitutional instruments of all thirteen original states — ten constitutions/declarations (1776–1780) plus the two colonial charters still in force as constitutions in 1776 (Connecticut 1662; Rhode Island 1663). Vermont's 1777 constitution was also surveyed and is recorded separately — Vermont was not one of the thirteen (admitted 1791) and is not counted in the thirteen-state figure. Of the thirteen, exactly one granted a "regulations" power over the militia: Pennsylvania 1776, Frame of Government, §5 — "The freemen of this commonwealth and their sons shall be trained and armed for its defence under such regulations, restrictions, and exceptions as the general assembly shall by law direct, preserving always to the people the right of choosing their colonels and all commissioned officers under that rank." Every other original state avoided the grant. The three instruments completing the set: Maryland (Constitution, November 11, 1776) — Declaration of Rights, Art. XXV uses "well-regulated militia" only descriptively ("That a well-regulated militia is the proper and natural defence of a free government"); Art. II reserves the instrument's sole "regulating" power — "the sole and exclusive right of regulating the internal government and police thereof" — to the people; Constitution, Art. XXXIII grants the Governor only command authority over the militia ("embody the militia" with Council consent; when embodied, "alone have the direction thereof"), plus officer appointment/suspension/removal (Art. XLVIII, XLV). Connecticut (Charter of 1662, April 23, 1662, in force as the constitution until 1818) — grants only the power "to Assemble, Martial-Array, and put in warlike Posture the Inhabitants of the said Colony" and to commission persons "to lead and conduct the said Inhabitants": command authority, not a regulate grant. Caveat (secondary-reported): a pre-revolutionary Connecticut statute (1712) is titled "An Act for Regulating the Militia" — a statute's title is not a constitutional power grant, and the charter in force as the constitution granted no regulate power; 1776–1792 Connecticut session laws were not swept (see F6). Rhode Island (Charter of July 1663, in force as the constitution until 1843) — grants only the power to nominate commanders and officers "for the leading, conductinge and travneing vpp the inhabitants... in martiall afiaires," with authority to "assemble, exercise in arms, martiall array, and putt in warlyke posture" them; the charter's one use of "regulate" concerns elections ("to regulate and order the wave and manner of all elections to offices and places of trust"), not the militia. The remaining instruments stand as previously recorded: New York (1777, Art. XL) used "armed and disciplined"; Massachusetts (1780) gave the governor power "to train, instruct, exercise and govern the militia"; the rest used "well regulated" only descriptively in rights-declarations or granted no militia power at all. Vermont (1777), separately labeled, granted the Pennsylvania-type power: Ch. II, §V directed that the freemen “shall be trained and armed for its defence, under such regulations, restrictions and exceptions, as the general assembly shall, by law, direct” — the administrative level, within the organize/arm/discipline family rather than the broad Clause 14 “regulate”; paired with the same express reservation to the people (“preserving always to the people, the right of choosing their colonels of militia, and all commissioned officers under that rank”). It stands as a second Pennsylvania-type counterexample with the same limits (1) (2); its subsequent history was not traced. The Pennsylvania counterexample, with its limits stated: (1) the grant covered "regulations, restrictions, and exceptions" for training and arming — the administrative level, arguably within the organize/arm/discipline family rather than the broad Clause-14 "regulate"; (2) it was paired with an express reservation to the people (officer elections); (3) it did not survive — Pennsylvania's 1790 constitution replaced it with "The freemen of this commonwealth shall be armed and disciplined for its defence...," dropping the "regulations" grant entirely, before the federal Bill of Rights; (4) as a federal Tenth Amendment matter, state-internal allocations do not alter the federal enumeration (see F6). Still open: Vermont 1777 carried forward, not re-verified; 1776–1792 Connecticut/Rhode Island session-law frameworks not swept; Maryland read via the Wikisource transcription of Thorpe (1909), corroborated against the Avalon snippet — the exact verbatim Avalon Maryland page was not reached; Rhode Island charter cited as "July 1663" to avoid asserting the disputed day (July 8 vs. July 15). 


F.6 The federal enactment ledger record (supports S8; see F5 for the full proposal text). The ledger's honest relocation: the claim moved from "no enactment" (false — Congress enacted militia statutes for 234 years) to "no declared end" (true — none produced "a well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State"). The full statute-by-statute ledger — Calling Forth Act 1792 (ch. 28; two-year sunset), Uniform Militia Act 1792 (ch. 33; enrollment plus "provide himself" self-arming), Militia Act 1795 (ch. 36; call-forth re-enacted without sunset), Act of March 3, 1807 (ch. 39; standing-force substitution), Act of April 23, 1808 (ch. 55; $200,000/year for arms "for the whole body of the militia," routed through the states), Militia Act 1862 (ch. 201; draft quotas; men of African descent), Dick Act 1903 (ch. 196; organized vs. reserve militia — the reserve received nothing), National Defense Act 1916 (ch. 134; federalized Guard; "unorganized militia" as definition, not force), 1933 amendments (ch. 87; Guard as federal reserve component) — is set out in F5's proposal text and not duplicated here. Each entry concedes the critic's best exhibits by name and citation, then shows each either armed the individual instead of the public, built a select/federal force instead of the general militia, or substituted regulars for the militia. Record notes not carried into the proposal text: the 1798 arms-for-sale Act (ch. 65 — 30,000 stands of arms to be sold to the states, secondary-reported) supports the burden-shift point and is available; the 1808 appropriation's later redirect would sharpen the select-militia point but the exact act was not identified — verify before citing; the "paper system" non-enforcement history of the 1792 Act is the standard historical account but was not sourced from a statute here — cite secondary literature, not the statute, if claimed. Still open: the 1916 ch./Stat. citation not independently verified (standard citation, secondary sourced); the Dick Act "repealed the 1792/1795 Acts" claim is Wikipedia-only — omitted unless verified; only the 1792 Uniform Militia Act was checked against a primary scan (govinfo.gov Statutes at Large) — all other statute texts are transcriptions on secondary hosts.


F.7 The Senate's "best" → "necessary" revision. The textual sequence is confirmed by modern government sources (Cornell LII; Congress.gov Constitution Annotated): Madison's June 8, 1789 draft — "the best security of a free country"; House version — "the best security of a free State"; Senate, September 9, 1789 — erased "best" and inserted "necessary to" after "being." Motive undocumented: no period newspaper discussion of the Senate's reason was located; the Senate Journal records the vote, not debate, and the Senate deliberated behind closed doors in this period. The strengthening from "best" to "necessary" is a textual fact; any claim about deliberate meaning requires evidence not yet found. Centinel date coincidence — flagged, not claimed: one law-review pinpoint dates the "it does not ordain" piece ("Centinel, Revived, No. XXIX") to September 9, 1789 — the same day as the Senate vote — but the piece quotes the House text ("best security") and could not comment on the Senate's change; no inference is drawn, and the July 2 vs. September 9 discrepancy must be resolved first (see F.3, F.12). 


F.8 "Public danger" lineage. A Cardozo Law Review article (vol. 36, 2015; search-excerpt — full article not read) traces the phrase through the English Civil War: Parliament's 1642 warning to Charles I of "public Dangers and Miseries"; the Militia Ordinance of 1642, "necessitated by a 'time of imminent danger'"; Parliament's "this Time of imminent and public Danger"; Charles I on "a Publick Danger." This supports treating "public danger" as an inherited term of art for extraordinary threats to the polity — broader than declared war, narrower than ordinary crime — consistent with the document's "public danger" analysis. It does not supply 1787–1792 American newspaper uses. Adjacent phrase — verified: the Pennsylvania minority proposal (December 12, 1787), item 7 of the minority’s bill of rights (Pennsylvania Packet, December 18, 1787), reads “...unless for crimes committed, or real danger of public injury from individuals” — “injury,” not “inquiry.”  Gap: no 1787–1792 newspaper uses of the exact Fifth Amendment phrase "public danger" were located. 


F.9 Modern scholarship ledger (contrary and complicating — recorded, not evaded). Heller's prefatory-clause holding: "Why So Silent? The Supreme Court and the Second Amendment Debate After DC v. Heller" (European Journal of American Studies, peer-reviewed) summarizes: Heller's majority concluded the prefatory clause did not "limit the right to militia service but simply 'announce[d] the purpose' for which the Amendment was written" — and that "virtually all interpreters of the Second Amendment in the century after its enactment interpreted the Amendment as we do." A standing contrary data point on the clause's office, though its historical survey's completeness is contested in the literature. (The document's command reading of the clause is stated in H1/H2.) Halbrook — the scholarly form of the Centinel problem: Stephen P. Halbrook, "To Keep and Bear Their Private Arms: The Adoption of the Second Amendment, 1787-1791" — "This indicates the understanding that the militia clause was merely declaratory and did not protect state rights to maintain militias to any appreciable degree. That anti-federalists of the ink of Centinel never attacked the right to bear arms clause demonstrates that it was considered to recognize a full and complete guarantee of individual rights to have and use private arms." Halbrook's reading and the document's reading of the same Centinel passage point in opposite directions about what the clause does, though both agree on the individual right to arms. This shows the contrary interpretation is held on originalist grounds, not only by modern gun-control scholarship. (See H1/H2.) The 1792 Act as strict-construction compromise (Indiana Magazine of History, peer-reviewed; search-excerpt): Congress "chose to interpret the Constitution strictly, and in the Militia Act of 1792 provided norms for the regulation of militia forces which respected state sensibilities" — after finding Knox's plan "appeared to contradict the Constitution's explicit reservation 'to the States respectively' of 'the Authority of training the Militia.'" Relevant both ways: it shows the generation took the clauses' limits seriously (support), but the limit it enforced was states' retained authority, and the compromise it produced was the self-arming act the document's ledger records (complicating). (See F5 for the ledger's treatment of the 1792 Act.) Knox plan's legislative history (MA thesis, Oakland University; search-excerpt; lower weight, but cites the standard historians Cress, Kohn, Kerby): the 1792 Act was a compromise after St. Clair's defeat (November 1791); the Federalists wanted federal "control, supply and discipline" — the public-provision position; the enacted act chose "thrift" — the self-arming burden (see F5 for the ledger's treatment). 


F.10 Knox plan reception record. The plan failed in Congress. Opposition is described in secondary sources as Republican/strict construction and state-autonomy based (1911 Encyclopædia Britannica: Knox "urged ineffectually a national militia system... and for this and his close friendship with Washington was bitterly assailed by the Republicans"). No period newspaper editorial or commentary on the plan was located. The administration's own "necessary institutions"/duty language (F.2) therefore stands as primary evidence of the plan's content, but its public reception is documented here only through later historians. The Documentary History of the First Federal Congress prints the full report (DHFC 5:1435–57), per the Founders Online editorial note.

Appendix G: The Plain Reading: What a Voter Sees in the Constitution
The Plain Reading: What a Voter Sees in the Constitution
Read the Constitution. Do not bring in court cases, old laws, or what anyone says it
means. Just read the words.
Here is what you see.
1. The Second Amendment says "A well regulated Militia."
Not militias. Not the several militias. Not a select guard. A militia. One.
2. It says "being necessary."
Not useful. Not helpful. Not eventual. Needed. Now.
3. "Well regulated" means governed by rules.
A militia without rules is not well regulated. So fulfilling the declaration requires
regulations.
4. Article I, Section 8, Clause 16 lists Congress's powers over the militia.
Congress can organize, arm, and discipline the militia. Clause 15 lets Congress call
the militia forth. Congress can govern the part employed in federal service. It does
not say Congress can regulate the militia.
5. Clause 14 uses the word "regulate" for land and naval forces. Clause 16 does not.
The same document uses the word in one place and leaves it out in the other. The
omission is not an accident. Congress was not given the power to regulate the militia.
**5a. The same section also has a clause saying Congress can make laws "necessary and
proper" for carrying out its powers.**
That clause is for carrying out powers Congress was given, not for creating powers it
was not given. It cannot supply a regulatory power the same section left out.
**6. The Tenth Amendment says powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited
to the States, are reserved to the States or to the People.**
The power to regulate the militia was not delegated to Congress. So it is reserved.
7. The States cannot do it individually.
If each state regulates the militia separately, you get fifty militias, not A
militia. The Constitution says A militia. Singular. National. One.
8. So the power to regulate is reserved to the People.
Not to Congress. Not to the States acting alone. To the People.
9. The Bill of Rights uses "the people" for things individuals do.
The First Amendment protects "the right of the people peaceably to assemble." The
Second protects "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms." The Fourth protects
"the right of the people to be secure." The Ninth says rights are "retained by the
people." In every case, "the people" includes individuals. There is no different meaning
in the Tenth Amendment.
**10. The Ninth Amendment says rights retained by the people shall not be denied or
disparaged.**
If the right to a well regulated militia cannot be fulfilled because no one can
exercise the power to regulate, the right is denied. The Ninth Amendment prohibits that.
11. "Necessary" does not wait.
If something is necessary, it is needed now. The free State cannot constitutionally
exist without a well regulated militia, so the absence of one is a constitutional
defect now — not eventually, not after further procedure. Delay is denial.
12. So an individual may supply the regulations the declared condition requires.
The individual is not making new law. The declaration already stands in supreme law.
The individual is supplying the content that fulfills it. This is fulfillment of the
declared condition, not the creation of new law.
13. The individual adds no new obligation.
The Constitution already declares the condition. The individual supplies the rules that
fulfill it. The authority comes from the declaration. The individual is the instrument.
14. Therefore these Regulations are the content the declared condition requires.
They stand because the declaration stands in supreme law. They are not new law. They
are the fulfillment of the declared condition.
The Objection
Someone will say: "The Constitution provides specific ways to make law. Article I says
how Congress makes laws. Article V says how the Constitution is amended. Article VII
says how it was ratified. Individual promulgation is not one of them."
The Answer
The individual is not making law. The declaration already stands. The individual is
fulfilling it.
If you say the declared condition cannot be fulfilled this way, cite the clause that
prohibits it. The Constitution nowhere says only Congress, only the States, or only a
collective body may supply the content the declared condition requires.
                                                               * The Tenth Amendment reserves the power to the People.
                                                               * The Ninth Amendment forbids making the right unfulfillable.
                                                               * The Second Amendment declares the militia necessary now.
So the individual exercise is the only remaining path. If you disagree, show where the
text prohibits it. If you cannot, the power is reserved, and the reservation is the
authorization.
What This Means
Read the Constitution. You see a declaration. You see the declared condition is unmet.
You see the power to fulfill it is reserved to the People. You see the People include
individuals. You see the Ninth Amendment forbids denial. You see necessary means now.
So an individual may provide the regulations. The individual is not a lawgiver. The
individual is a servant of the declared condition. The declaration is supreme law. The
regulations are the fulfillment.
That is the plain reading. Read it yourself.












Founders' Warnings Ignored by Modern Government
                                                               * Hamilton (Fed. No. 29): Standing armies are "dangerous to liberty."
                                                               * Jefferson (Letter to Madison, 1787): "Paper money is immoral."
                                                               * Madison (Fed. No. 45): Federal powers "few and defined."
                                                               * Washington (Farewell Address, 1796): "Avoid the accumulation of debt... throwing upon posterity burdens we ought to bear."
                                                               * Benjamin Franklin (1755): Those who trade liberty for safety "deserve neither."
                                                               * James Wilson (Lectures on Law, 1791): "Taxes should be levied conspicuously", "Gold and silver... are the only proper measures of commerce."
                                                               * Luther Martin (Genuine Information, 1787): States must retain powers not "expressly surrendered" to avoid "consolidated tyranny."
                                                               * Elbridge Gerry (House Debate, 1789): Standing armies are "engines of despotism"; the militia is the people's "sole safe defense."
                                                               * Samuel Adams (Letter to James Warren, 1776): "Where knowledge is diffused... tyrants and tyrannical laws will dread to attack."
                                                               * "The tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time with the blood of patriots & tyrants." - Jefferson 1787.
                                                               * James Madison (Federalist No. 44, 1788): “Had the Constitution been silent on this head, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers requisite as means of executing the general powers would have resulted to the government by unavoidable implication. … The necessary and proper clause is merely declaratory of a truth which would have resulted by necessary and unavoidable implication from the very act of constituting a federal government.”
                                                               * Alexander Hamilton (Federalist No. 33, 1788): “If it be asked, what is to be the consequence, in case the Congress shall misconstrue this part of the Constitution, and exercise powers not warranted by its true meaning? … It is the people who, in the last resort, must determine the controversy.




















Marbury v. Madison 1803 -  “All Laws which are repugnant to the constitution are null and void” - Chief Justice John Marshall, emphasized that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land and that any legislative act that contradicts it is void.
Formal Declaration of Constitutional Restoration
Issued by the Free State Militia
Under the Authority of the U.S. Constitution (1787–1791)
Sovereign Proclamation
To All Occupants of Federal and State Governments:
The United States Constitution, ratified by the People as the supreme Law of the Land (Article VI, Clause 2), binds every official to its original intent. You have violated this sacred covenant through deliberate acts of usurpation, undermining the free state—a condition where the Constitution reigns, individual liberties are inviolate, and powers not delegated remain with the States or the People (Ninth and Tenth Amendments). Your actions are treasonous, rendering your authority null and void.
WHEREAS:
                                                               * You have defied Article I, Section 10 by imposing fiat currency, such as Federal Reserve notes, in place of gold and silver coin, the only lawful tender.
                                                               * You have usurped the militia’s exclusive authority under Article I, Section 8, Clause 15 to execute the Laws of the Union, allowing unauthorized agencies (e.g., FBI, ATF, DHS) to operate in its stead.
                                                               * You have trampled the Ninth and Tenth Amendments, seizing powers reserved to the States and the People, eroding the free state’s foundation.
YOU ARE DECLARED USURPERS, stripped of legitimacy. The Free State Militia, as the People’s constitutional guardian, now acts to restore the free state.
Article I: Violations
Your crimes against the Constitution are as follows:
                                                               * Treasonous Currency: Enforcing fiat currency violates Article I, Section 10, robbing the People of their economic sovereignty.
                                                               * Unlawful Enforcement: Permitting non-militia entities to execute federal law defies Article I, Section 8, Clause 15, threatening the free state’s security.
                                                               * Oath Betrayal: Your failure to uphold your Article VI oath forfeits the authority on which your offices rest (§13.2.1(c)); removal follows through the constitutional mechanisms (§13.3). 
                                                               * Property Theft: Seizures of property through the fiat currency system — established in 8.5–8.6 as constitutionally unauthorized — violate the Fifth Amendment. Taxation is an exercise of delegated power under Article I, Section 8, Clause 1, not a taking. The constitutional objections to the federal tax system lie in the Fifth Amendment’s prohibition on compelled self-incrimination and in the apportionment requirement of Article I, Section 9, Clause 4.
Refer to the Regulations of the Free State Militia for a full explanation. 
Article II: Demands
To restore constitutional order, the Free State Militia demands immediate compliance:
Federal Officials: Affirm your oath to the Constitution by ceasing enforcement of all unconstitutional systems identified herein, or resign all offices. Upon resignation, you forfeit claim to pensions and benefits derived from oath-breaking service, but retain all personal property lawfully acquired. Your person remains secure; your property remains yours.
State Officials: Repeal all statutes recognizing Federal Reserve notes as legal tender, or resign your offices. State treasury assets held in fiat form shall be converted to gold and silver coin through constitutional transition mechanisms as described in Section 8.5.12. No personal assets of state officials or employees shall be seized.
All Agencies: Disband immediately. Equipment and facilities purchased with federal funds shall be transferred, not seized, to State-appointed Militia command per Section 8.5.7 part (e). No personal property of any employee shall be taken. Employees who resign or cooperate in orderly transition shall retain all personal effects, retirement accounts, and private assets.
To All Citizens: Your savings, your bank accounts, your retirement funds, your wages, your homes, your digital assets, all are absolutely protected. Section 8.5.9 is not negotiable. The Militia exists to defend you, not to plunder you.
Failure to comply will trigger enforcement actions targeting institutional and senior policy-making violators only, per the strict criteria of Section 13.5.5, and only after all peaceful remedies have been exhausted and documented as required by Section 4.8.1.
Article III: Constitutional Defense of the free state
Detention Authority: The Fifth Amendment's explicit exception for "cases arising in the Militia during public danger" provides constitutional text authorizing temporary defensive detention of usurpers.


You have infringed upon the free state, the Free State Militia will enact the following:
                                                               * Nullification: All state and federal laws, orders, and directives issued by all free state infringers are void.

Article IV: Constitutional Authority
This Declaration is rooted in:
                                                               * Second Amendment: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State,” mandates our duty to eliminate threats to liberty.
                                                               * Tenth Amendment: Undelegated powers belong to the States or the People, authorizing our action against your overreach.
                                                               * Declaration of Independence (1776): The People’s right to abolish destructive governance underpins our resolve.
Tyranny invites destruction; liberty demands defense.
Article V: Resistance to Infringement
Any attempt to disarm the People, obstruct our constitutional duties, or infringe the free state will be deemed an act of war against the Constitution. The Free State Militia will respond with overwhelming force:
                                                               * Disarmament Efforts: Seizure or restriction of arms will be met with immediate armed resistance.

We seek restoration, not bloodshed, but we will not hesitate to bear arms against those who infringe upon the free state if forced to. The People’s liberty is non-negotiable.
Article VI: A Path of Inclusion for Officers of the Republic
To All Federal and State Officials Bound by Oath:
The Free State Militia, as the armed People of the United States rising under the U.S. Constitution (1787–1791), addresses you not merely as adversaries but as fellow citizens once entrusted with the sacred duty to preserve the free state—a lawful order where the Constitution reigns supreme, individual liberties stand inviolate, and powers not delegated remain with the States or the People (Ninth and Tenth Amendments).                                                                * Article I, Section 10: Ensuring only gold and silver coin serve as legal tender, a mandate you have betrayed by endorsing fiat currency.
